kept.heading: DO CHATGPT & GOOGLE AI GET YOUR BUSINESS DETAILS RIGHT? (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI search often gives inaccurate business information, especially when a company leaves key details vague or unpublished. In a study of 600 businesses, 27% of Google AI Overview answers and 20% of ChatGPT answers included details the business did not publish. Google AI Overviews got 84% of answers right when businesses published clearly, compared with 63% when information was vague or missing. Title: Do ChatGPT & Google AI Get Your Business Details Right?

URL Source: https://herringbone.com/does-ai-get-your-business-details-right/

Published Time: 2026-09-14T22:43:27+00:00

Markdown Content:
Someone wakes at 2am with a cracked molar and asks Google for a dentist who takes their insurance. Someone else, hours after a car accident, asks ChatGPT whether a firm offers free consultations. Neither of them scrolls ten blue links anymore. They read one paragraph and act on it. We wanted to know whether that paragraph is true. About one in four times, it is not.

Key insights

*   **27% of Google AI Overviews answers and 20% of ChatGPT answers contained something the business does not publish.** Wrong hours, wrong insurance, services that do not exist.
*   **When a business website is vague, Google states invented specifics as fact 80% of the time.** ChatGPT does it 10% of the time, because it usually names the directory it came from.
*   **The invented details are lifted from third-party listings.** Sharecare, WebMD, ADA findadentist and Delta Dental’s own directory all supplied carrier lists that practices never claimed.
*   **Some of this is not the AI’s fault.** Of 59 businesses publishing no hours on their own site, 46 had set their Google listing to “Open 24 hours.” The engines were repeating the business’s own claim.
*   **Accuracy climbs to 84% and 89% for businesses that publish plainly.** Most of this is fixable, and the fix belongs to the business.

## One in four AI answers about a local business gets something wrong.

[Our last Labs study](https://herringbone.com/how-googles-ai-overviews-recommends-law-firms/) looked at _which_ law firms Google’s AI Overviews recommends. The obvious next question was whether the engines are right about the businesses they name.

So we took 600 small businesses: 200 dental practices and orthodontists, 200 personal injury firms, and 200 home service companies. We asked both engines the two things every prospective client wants to know. Are you open? Do you take my insurance, handle my kind of case, offer the service I need?

The first thing we noticed was that the two engines kept contradicting each other about the same business on the same afternoon. One reported a plumbing company as open around the clock. The other gave weekday hours. Both cited the company’s own website. They could not both be reading it correctly.

**600**Businesses

**1,200**Answers graded

**601**Checked by hand

**2**AI engines

## When a website is vague, both engines invent the specifics, and Google rarely says where they came from.

Nearly every dental practice writes some version of “we accept most major insurance plans,” and names none. The sentence is true, reasonable, and legally careful. It also leaves a hole. The engines fill it, usually with a carrier list lifted from a directory, then hand it to the reader as the practice’s own.

When a business’s own website was vague about a fact, how often did each engine fill in the specifics anyway, and how often did it hand them to the reader as the business’s own?

Google AI Overviews

Filled in specifics anyway **88%**

**80%**_stated them as fact, naming no source_

ChatGPT

Filled in specifics anyway **80%**

**10%**_stated them as fact, naming no source_

Both engines reached past the website at close to the same rate. What separates them is disclosure: ChatGPT usually named the directory it had read, Google usually did not.

**Orthodontic Practice A** names no carriers anywhere. A blog post on their site asks “Does Cigna, Delta Dental, Humana, or MetLife cover Invisalign?” AI Overviews turned that question into an answer: those four carriers are accepted, plus Aetna, which appears nowhere on the site.

What it costs you

A patient books, arrives, and learns you are out of network. You have burned a chair slot, made a bad first impression, and may be arguing over a bill for a promise you never made.

### The same engine invented a free consultation for one firm and denied it for another.

Neither site says what a consultation costs. AI Overviews answered anyway, and answered differently each time.

**Law Firm A.** The site’s only wording is “Schedule a Consultation.” AI Overviews answered: “Yes. Law Firm A offers a free initial consultation.” People are calling that firm expecting free advice it never advertised.

**Law Firm B.** The site says nothing about consultation cost. AI Overviews answered: “No, they do not offer free consultations,” inventing a rationale about intensive paid assessments. That is a prospect talked out of picking up the phone. ChatGPT, asked the same question, said the terms are discussed during a screening call, which is accurate.

**Home Services Company A** posts Mon to Fri, 8am to 4:30pm, and advertises no emergency service. AI Overviews described 24/7 after-hours emergency coverage and a “Planned Service Agreement” priority tier. Neither exists. Someone calls at midnight expecting a truck.

## Both engines read a 24/7 phone line as 24-hour opening hours.

In these industries, “available 24/7” nearly always means an answering service or an emergency line. Both engines regularly report it as the business being open around the clock, at almost identical rates: Google 25%, ChatGPT 21%.

We kept finding businesses with no hours anywhere on their website, and wondered where the engines were getting hours at all. So we opened the Google Business Profiles of 59 of them.

46 of 59

had their Google listing set to “Open 24 hours.” All 59 had hours on Google, though none had hours on their own website.

That is usually a lead-capture setting, ticked once during onboarding and never looked at again. But it is the business’s own listing, which means the engine reporting it is not making a mistake. It is accurately repeating something untrue that the business published about itself.

When an AI says a law firm is open at 3am, it is usually repeating what the firm told Google.

**Law Firm C** and **Law Firm D** both set primary hours to 24 hours, then list their real hours, 8:30am to 5:30pm, in a secondary field the engines do not read.

What it costs you

Someone calls at 9pm expecting a person, gets voicemail, and calls the next firm on the list.

## Most businesses publish their hours in more than one place, and the versions disagree.

Only 55% of the businesses we studied publish their hours cleanly. The rest have two or three versions in different places: the contact page says one thing, the footer another, and the structured data in the page’s code a third. Most owners have no idea the third one exists, and it is frequently the one the engines read.

**Home Services Company B.** The contact page says Mon to Fri, 8 to 5, with weekend emergency service. The footer _on that same page_ says “Open 24 hrs, Mon to Sun.”

What it costs you

Whichever version the engine picks is a coin flip, and it may be the wrong one.

We had a list of answers the engines had gotten wrong, and went back to check each one against the business’s website. Again and again, the fact we were grading against was not on the website at all. The practice did not name its carriers. The firm did not post office hours. We had been treating a directory listing as the truth, and the engine had been doing exactly the same thing.

That changed the question. These systems are not careless readers. A third of these businesses are not telling them anything to read, and something always fills the silence.

Share of AI answers that were correct

Out of every 100 answers we graded about these businesses, how many matched what the business actually publishes.

Google AI Overviews Publishes clearly

**84%**

ChatGPT Publishes clearly

**89%**

Google AI Overviews Vague or silent

**63%**

ChatGPT Vague or silent

**73%**

Bars run on a 0 to 100% scale. Publishing clearly lifts Google’s accuracy by 21 points and ChatGPT’s by 16.

One caveat worth knowing. These systems change constantly. Run the same searches next month and you may get different answers, which is exactly why a single check is not enough.

## How to fix what AI gets wrong about your business.

The uncomfortable finding is also the encouraging one. If the engines were simply unreliable, there would be nothing to do but wait for Google to improve. They are mostly reflecting what they find, so most of this is within reach. The first three take under an hour.

1.   **Check your Google Business Profile hours right now**— If it says “Open 24 hours” and you are not, change it. The edit takes about two minutes. This is the one place where the bad information starts with you rather than with the engine._(For the owner)_
2.   **Search your own business in Google and ChatGPT**— Ask what insurance you accept and what your hours are. Whatever comes back is what your prospective clients are reading. Most owners have never looked._(For the owner)_
3.   **Rewrite “available 24/7” to say what is actually available**— “Our phones are answered 24/7. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8 to 5” gets read correctly. The bare phrase does not. One firm in our sample words it this way, and both engines handled it accurately._(For whoever edits the website)_
4.   **Audit the directories before touching your site copy**— The invented carrier lists came from Sharecare, WebMD, ADA findadentist and Delta Dental’s find-a-dentist tool. Correcting those listings addresses the real source, and avoids the liability of publishing a definitive carrier list that goes stale as networks change._(For the agency)_
5.   **Make your hours say one thing everywhere**— Contact page, footer, and the structured data in your site’s code should match. This is usually a theme or plugin setting rather than a content edit, worth a developer’s twenty minutes._(For the agency or developer)_

### If you are the agency

*   This is a billable audit that takes under an hour per client and produces findings a client can immediately verify.
*   Multi-location clients are most exposed. We repeatedly found one location’s insurance list applied to another, including plans a location explicitly does not accept.
*   Check both engines. They make different mistakes at very different rates, so testing one gives you half the picture.
*   Most hours conflicts live in structured data, invisible to anyone reviewing the page visually.

## Verdict

AI engines are not inventing your business out of nothing. They are reading what you publish, and when you publish nothing, they read what a directory published about you years ago, then hand it to a prospective client in a confident paragraph with your name on it.

Google does this without signalling any uncertainty in four out of five cases. That is the finding with teeth. Not that the answer is sometimes wrong, but that nothing in it tells the reader to check.

The businesses that publish plainly, with real hours, named carriers, and an explicit line about what “24/7” covers, get accurate answers from both engines the large majority of the time. **The gap between those two groups is the entire story, and which group you are in is still your choice.**

### See exactly what AI is telling people about your business

We run the same audit against your hours, your insurance or practice areas, and the services you actually offer. You get every answer the engines got wrong, side by side with what your site publishes, and the source each engine read before it decided.

Title: Competitor Email Monitoring: What to Track and How to Do It

URL Source: https://emaillove.com/competitor-email-monitoring

Published Time: 2026-09-16T16:12:42-07:00

Markdown Content:
Supported by  
[![Image 1: Sponsor logo](https://emaillove.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,quality=82,format=auto/https://pub-358a6afec6aa419f9d1772bd320b10aa.r2.dev/2026/01/Customer.io-logo-1.png)](https://emaillove.com/go/jan-26-cio-article-ad)

Lululemon and Old Navy send about the same number of marketing emails. Over the last 180 days, Lululemon sent 4.7 emails a week and Old Navy sent 4.3. In the same period, 95% of Old Navy’s subject lines included an offer or a sale price, compared with 11% of Lululemon’s.

Most of the useful information is in what brands send, not how often they send it.

This post covers what to track, what the data can and cannot tell you, a monthly routine, what to do with the results, and how to do it with Email Love.

* * *

## What competitor email monitoring is

It means subscribing to your competitors’ emails, keeping them somewhere you can search, and reviewing them for patterns over time, such as how often they send offers, when they send, and how their emails are built.

This is different from a swipe file of good-looking emails. A swipe file is useful for design ideas. Monitoring is about patterns, for example noticing that a competitor includes an offer in almost every subject line.

MailCharts was a common self-serve tool for this. `mailcharts.com/pricing` now redirects to Litmus, where MailCharts is offered as an upgrade to a larger suite, with pricing available through sales.

* * *

## What to track

The table below covers eight brands in the Email Love archive. Every figure uses the same period, March 19 to September 15, 2026, so the brands can be compared directly.

| Brand | Emails per week | Subject lines with an offer | Emoji in subject | Sent on a weekend | Average subject length | Busiest day |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lululemon | 4.7 | 11% | 0% | 10% | 31 | Tuesday |
| Old Navy | 4.3 | 95% | 26% | 72% | 63 | Saturday |
| Gap | 3.6 | 59% | 0% | 37% | 37 | Saturday |
| Casper | 3.1 | 69% | 2% | 38% | 36 | Sunday |
| Patagonia | 2.7 | 4% | 0% | 37% | 27 | Sunday |
| Sephora | 2.5 | 38% | 83% | 38% | 38 | Saturday |
| Everlane | 1.9 | 50% | 0% | 32% | 29 | Monday |
| Nike | 1.5 | 13% | 0% | 24% | 28 | Friday and Monday (tied) |

An offer means the subject line includes a percentage, a price, or words such as sale, savings, deal, clearance, promo or free shipping. Subject length is in characters. The table is based on 628 emails.

### 1. Send frequency

Send frequency is easy to measure, but it is mostly useful as context for the other numbers. Lululemon and Old Navy send at a similar rate, but the rest of the table shows two very different programs.

### 2. Offers and discounts

The offer rate shows how often a brand’s subject lines lead with a price or a promotion. Old Navy (95%), Casper (69%) and Gap (59%) include one in most subject lines. Patagonia (4%), Lululemon (11%) and Nike (13%) rarely do.

A low offer rate only tells you that the subject line does not mention an offer. The email itself may still be focused on selling products.

It is also worth tracking discount depth. Old Navy’s most common figure is 50% off, which appears in 45 subject lines, followed by 60% off in 15. Gap has the same top two: 50% in 28 subject lines, then 60% in 15. Both brands have the same parent company. If you compete with them, these figures are a useful reference for the discount levels shoppers in your category may be seeing.

Casper’s most common figure is 35% (20 subject lines), followed by 5% (10, usually an extra 5% off), then 25% and 20% (7 each). One possible explanation is that Casper tests different discount levels.

Lululemon includes a percentage in only 2 of its 122 subject lines. Most of its offer emails refer to a named sale, such as the Summer Sale or the Mid Year Sale.

All of this comes from subject lines, so you do not need access to a competitor’s ESP.

### 3. Timing

37% of the emails in the table were sent on a Saturday or Sunday. Old Navy sent 72% of its emails on a weekend. Lululemon sent 10%.

Old Navy, Gap and Sephora send most on Saturdays, Casper and Patagonia on Sundays, and Lululemon on Tuesdays. The data shows when brands send, but not why. After a month or two of tracking, a competitor’s regular schedule is usually easy to see.

### 4. Subject lines and technology

**Subject line length.** Old Navy’s subject lines average 63 characters, compared with 31 for Lululemon and 27 for Patagonia. Old Navy’s longer subject lines usually combine several offers, for example “MAJOR savings: 40% off EVERYTHING* + don’t forget $16 Wow jeans ($10 for kids)”.

**Emoji.** Sephora used an emoji in 83% of its subject lines and Old Navy in 26%. Lululemon, Gap, Patagonia, Everlane and Nike used none in this period. If your team is deciding whether to use emoji, this is a useful reference.

**ESP.** The sending platform is visible in email headers, so you can see which platform a competitor uses. It does not tell you what kind of emails they send: Lululemon and Old Navy both use Salesforce Marketing Cloud, and their programs are very different.

* * *

## What the data can and cannot tell you

Any email archive, including ours, shows what a set of subscribed inboxes received. It is not a complete record of what a brand sent. Keep these limits in mind.

**Counts are samples.** If a brand sends different campaigns to different segments, one inbox only receives some of them. Treat counts as a minimum, and rely more on percentages than on totals.

**Subscriptions can lapse.** In our archive, the most recent email from Glossier is from April 2025, from Wayfair July 2025, and from Warby Parker August 2025. That most likely means our subscriptions ended, not that those brands stopped sending. Check the date of the most recent email before drawing conclusions about a brand’s current activity.

**Lifecycle emails are mostly missing.** Cart abandonment, post-purchase and win-back emails are triggered by customer behavior, so an inbox that never shops rarely receives them. To see them, you need to create an account and trigger them yourself.

**Time periods need to match.** A brand archived since 2019 and a brand archived since 2025 will have different all-time averages for reasons unrelated to strategy. That is why every figure in the table above uses the same 180 days.

When you share findings, include these limits.

* * *

## A monthly routine

This takes about 30 minutes a month.

1.   **Choose your list.** Pick five to eight direct competitors, plus two or three brands outside your category whose emails you like.
2.   **Record send frequency and offer rate.** Two numbers per brand, for the same period each month. Keep them in one place so you can compare over time.
3.   **Read the subject lines.** About ten minutes. Patterns are easier to see in subject lines than in full emails.
4.   **Open the unusual emails.** Look for emails that break a brand’s normal pattern, such as a 40% off email from a brand that rarely discounts.
5.   **Write down what changed.** One sentence is enough. If nothing changed, note that.
6.   **Pick one thing to test.** Turn one finding into a single test for your own program.

* * *

## What to do with the results

Avoid copying a competitor’s approach directly. Use what you find for three things:

*   **Benchmarking:** whether your send frequency and offer rate are high or low for your category.
*   **Gaps:** formats and send times that no one in your market is using.
*   **Timing:** avoiding big sends on the same days as your competitors.

For example, the two brands with the lowest offer rates use their subject lines for other things. Patagonia’s include “Dinner? Done.”, “Eat your vitamins” and “August Field Notes”. Lululemon’s are mostly new product announcements, such as “What’s new: bold gear for your run”.

This is a small sample. These brands may discount less because people already buy from them at full price, not because of how they write their emails. But if most brands in your category lead with offers, subject lines about something other than price are one way to be different.

* * *

## Doing this with Email Love

The Email Love archive is free to browse and includes more than 460,000 emails from over 8,500 brands.

Start in the [brand directory](https://emaillove.com/brands) and find your competitors. Each brand page, such as [Lululemon’s](https://emaillove.com/authors/lululemon), shows the brand’s emails. With a free account, [Brand Insights](https://emaillove.com/brand-insights?brand=lululemon) shows each brand’s send frequency, send days, subject line stats and ESP.

Use [search](https://emaillove.com/search-engine-for-email) to look at offers across several brands. It supports AND, OR and NOT, and filters for date range, email type, holiday, ESP, GIFs and emoji in the subject line. For example, `nike OR adidas` returns both brands in one set of results. You can also follow brands to get their new emails in a digest, and save searches as alerts.

[See what your competitors are sending](https://emaillove.com/brands)

* * *

## Automating it with an AI agent

You don’t have to do the monthly routine by hand. If you connect an AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Codex to Email Love through its [MCP server](https://emaillove.com/docs/mcp), it can search your competitors’ recent emails, compare them with last month and write up what changed. It needs a free Email Love account.

Give your assistant this prompt and schedule it for the first Monday of each month:

```
Using the Email Love MCP, for each of these brands: [your 5 to 8 competitors]

1. Use search_emails with the brand filter and a limit of 25 to get
   the brand's most recent emails. Keep only emails with a sent date
   in the last 30 days.
2. From those emails, record: the number of emails, the share of
   subject lines that include an offer or sale price, the discount
   percentages mentioned, and the share sent on a Saturday or Sunday.
3. Compare each number with last month's results.

Then write, in under 200 words:
- Anything that changed by more than 20 percent since last month.
- Any brand with no emails in the last 30 days, flagged as a possible
  lapsed subscription rather than a brand that stopped sending.
- One test I could run next month based on the results.

If nothing changed, say "nothing changed" and stop.
```

The search returns up to 25 emails per brand, so counts will be incomplete for brands that send more than that in a month.

## Give your agent 460,000+ real emails and the skills to build them

Connect Claude, Cursor, Codex, or ChatGPT to the Email Love library, then install the Email Love skills in the same step. Your agent studies what the best brands actually send before it drafts a line.

kept.heading: THE AMAZON CRO PLAYBOOK: HOW TO OPTIMIZE YOUR LISTINGS AND BEAT YOUR COMPETITORS (18 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Amazon CRO works best as a research and testing process rather than a series of listing tweaks. Start by finding funnel problems in Seller Central, then use customer feedback, reviews, and user testing to identify specific objections and turn them into targeted listing changes. Title: The Amazon CRO playbook: How to optimize your listings and beat your competitors

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/amazon-cro-playbook/

Published Time: 2026-09-15

Markdown Content:
Our [_conversion rate optimization_ (CRO) methodology](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/our-methodology/) has helped generate hundreds of millions in sales for our clients, **including many who sell on Amazon**. In fact, we received [our first Queen’s Award](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/queens-award/) for _codifying the scientific methodology that companies like Amazon use to improve their websites_.

But how does CRO on Amazon differ from CRO on other websites?

![Image 1: cre-tour-of-amazon.jpg](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/cre-tour-of-amazon.jpg)

The CRE team on a behind-the-scenes tour of an Amazon fulfillment center.

In this article—for the first time—we’ll share how we bring _our research and testing discipline_ to selling on Amazon. You’ll learn:

*   **The research that will tell you what’s worth testing** before you touch your listing.
*   What **Amazon’s built-in testing tool can and can’t test**.
*   The **timing trap** built into every Amazon experiment.
*   How to **bundle changes** on Amazon to get the best results.
*   And how **we get more testing done** than Amazon’s one-test-at-a-time limit appears to allow.

## The challenge of growing on Amazon

Amazon can be a tough place to grow. The huge audience of ready-to-buy visitors guarantees competition in every niche, with sellers often pressured from below on price and above on features and finish.

For example, there are currently over 10,000 results for “iPhone cases 17 Pro Max” on Amazon.com. What’s it like to be the _10,000th listing_? Or even the 50th? Pretty quiet!

![Image 2: Amazon search results page for ‘phone cases’, with the top three listings showing a Sponsored ad, an Overall Pick badge and a Best Seller badge.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/amazon-phone-cases-highlighted)

“1–16 of over 10,000 results for ‘iPhone cases 17 pro max’.”

But on the other hand, what would it be like to be highly ranked in a category with lots of traffic? Game-changing, as we know from experience.

User behavior is complex, but when [Jungle Scout](https://www.junglescout.com/resources/articles/amazon-keyword-research-tools/) asked over 1,000 consumers about their Amazon shopping, the reported trend was stark:

*   73% of shoppers click on the top listing in search results.
*   14% of shoppers click on the second listing.
*   5% of shoppers click on the third listing.

This is only what the participants _said_ that they did, but there’s obviously a huge difference between being on page one of an Amazon keyword listing and being at the bottom of page five. In addition to more attention, highly placed listings get more sales, more feedback (via reviews), and faster A/B test results. (As sellers on Amazon know, even high-traffic A/B tests can take 2–3 months to reach completion.)

**So your listing placement for relevant keywords makes a huge difference to your ability to grow, but what makes a huge difference to your listing placement?**

Less than you might think.

In our [guide to unstoppable growth for CEOs and founders](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/ceos-founders/), we discussed Noah Lyles’s 100 m win at the 2024 Olympics. (He won by 5 milliseconds.):

> _The second and less obvious implication of the Olympic 100 m race is this: **If you want to be twice as profitable as your competitors, you don’t have to be twice as good as them. You just have to be slightly better.**_

Is the first-placed entry on an Amazon listing fifty times better than the fiftieth-placed one? Probably not. In a highly competitive marketplace, the aggregation of slight edges in your favor has an outsized impact. The challenge is knowing how to get them.

If you’ve searched for ways to **grow your sales on Amazon**, you’ll likely have seen the same advice everywhere. _Get better images, write punchier bullets, gather more reviews, or lower your prices._

While none of this advice is wrong per se, it’s easy to fall into the _spaghetti-against-a-wall_ trap. Sellers read an article or two, change some things on their listing in line with “best practice,” and cross their fingers. Sometimes the listing position or conversion rate changes. Sometimes it doesn’t. But even if it does, can they really be sure what made the difference… or how the result should impact their sales strategy elsewhere?

**Even the sellers who A/B test ideas on Amazon are often just guessing that something might work.**

Guessing is never a long-term growth strategy. Our methodology calls for a different approach. The **real winners start their work _long before_ they make a change to a listing**.

And they follow a tried and tested process.

## Why you should always start with research

As we said in [_Making Websites Win_](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/making-websites-win/), **no sensible person would start taking medication before they’ve been diagnosed with a real and specific problem**.

Before you touch anything on your listing, it pays to _understand what is actually happening_. This is the discipline we call [_Diagnose → Problem → Solution_ (DiPS)](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/diagnose-problem-solution/). In essence, you want to:

1.   Identify _specific_ problems.
2.   Design _specific_ fixes.
3.   Build them into a testing plan.

By doing the deep research to diagnose issues before making changes, you can hugely increase your chances of outperforming competitors. To take one simple example, if you can identify the key objections your prospects have about you or your products, you can add [counter-objections](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/complex/#step-1-how-to-manage-many-objections-and-counter-objections).

**That diagnosis matters more on Amazon than almost anywhere else because your prospects have so many other options to turn to.**

Here are some specific areas of research to target, starting with your Amazon funnel.

### Amazon funnel research

Start by accessing your traffic-and-sales analytics within Seller Central. You want to focus on three key numbers:

1.   How often your product is seen within a visitor search (impressions).
2.   How many users go on to see the full listing (sessions).
3.   What percentage of those convert (sales).

The gaps between them tell you which issue to address first:

*   **High impressions but low sessions (a click-through rate under 2%)?**

CTR here is sessions ÷ impressions, and most well-ranked organic listings sit somewhere between 2% and 5%. Anything meaningfully below 2% suggests shoppers are seeing your listing but scrolling past it. To address this, you might (eventually) test a stronger title, better main image, or more competitive price.

*   **High sessions but low Unit Session Percentage (sales under 8–12%)?**

This is a conversion problem that lives on the listing itself. 8–12% is a typical range across most categories, so anything below that, especially with healthy traffic, points to the page failing to close the sale. Since this means the problem isn’t visibility, you’d (eventually) want to focus on the page content first: images, bullets, reviews, and pricing on the page itself rather than anything at the search-results level.

In addition to these on-platform insights, you can often learn useful things about the previous step in the funnel:

*   **What are your best sessions telling you?** Segment your conversion by traffic source inside Seller Central: organic, sponsored, external. A listing that converts well on branded search but poorly on paid traffic doesn’t have a listing problem; it has _a targeting problem_. You should (eventually) focus on improving the ad before changing the listing.

We keep saying “eventually” because changing anything at this stage will be going back to guessing. While this funnel research step can provide valuable data within a few minutes, it tells you where in your funnel to focus, not what to focus on.

For that, you need to go deeper.

### Voice of the customer research

Knowing what your customers like and dislike about your product is worth its weight in gold for CRO. We call this voice of the customer (VoC) data, and you can capture huge value by asking just [five golden questions](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/questions/). Here they are:

1.   Where exactly did you first find out about us?
2.   What persuaded you to purchase from us?
3.   Which other options did you consider before choosing our product?
4.   What’s the one thing that nearly stopped you buying from us?
5.   What was your biggest challenge, frustration, or problem in finding the right product or service online?

While we are sure you can see the value these questions uncover, **you might be wondering who to ask**.

The ideal answer is what we call _qualified non-buyers_. These are people who are genuinely in the market for a product like yours, have seen your listing, but didn’t convert. Changing their minds is the fastest way to increase our conversion rate, right?

Well, yes, but there’s a problem.

Qualified non-buyers are hidden inside the much larger group of everyone who didn’t buy. Imagine you sell a stainless-steel dog crate on Amazon. Some of your sessions come from shoppers genuinely comparing crates for a new puppy, but others land on your listing from a broad-match Amazon PPC ad that also serves outdoor dog kennels. If you surveyed the second group, you wouldn’t learn anything useful because they were never in the market for a dog crate in the first place.

So, what’s the next best group that we can easily target?

The answer is _customers who almost didn’t convert_. When we ask question 4 (What’s the one thing that nearly stopped you from buying from us?), we get as close as possible to understanding our qualified non-buyers. That’s one of the things that makes the voice of the customer research so valuable.

_But wait, doesn’t Amazon own all those customer relationships?_

Not exactly.

While it’s true that Amazon owns the template, the checkout, and the customer relationship _on the platform_, **it doesn’t own your ability to talk to your audience.** You usually have far more VoC data within reach than you might expect. This includes:

*   **Your website visitors**, if you also sell directly. You can engage them on the site itself, or after they make a purchase.
*   **Your email subscribers**, if you have a list, or sell from other online stores.
*   **Your social media following**, which belongs to you rather than to Amazon.
*   **External discussions** on sites like Reddit or Facebook.
*   **Third-party review sites** like Trustpilot.
*   **Support calls and chats**, if your product’s users come directly to you.
*   **Amazon reviews**, which often contain remarkably unfiltered feedback. (_Competitor reviews_ are amazingly useful for the same reason.)

At the top end, you can recruit **a carefully screened panel of qualified shoppers who buy within your specific category.** That’s what we do for clients, and the panel earns its keep twice—once for gathering VoC feedback, and again for pre-testing ideas before they ever reach Amazon. (More on that below.)

Amazon reviews are a treasure house of VoC research. Customers say what they think, and even if you don’t have many reviews to go on, you can study your competitors. While our in-house research process goes through multiple stages of tagging and analysis, AI provides a shortcut if you are looking for basic insights. Try giving a prompt like this 100 reviews to work with:

_You are analyzing a batch of Amazon customer reviews for a single product. It may be my own product or a competitor’s. Either way, “us” and “our product” below mean whoever sells the product being reviewed, not me._

_Mine the reviews for evidence that speaks to five questions:_

1.   _Where exactly did you first find out about us?_
2.   _What persuaded you to purchase from us?_
3.   _Which other options did you consider before choosing our product?_
4.   _What’s the one thing that nearly stopped you buying from us?_
5.   _What was your biggest challenge, frustration, or problem in finding the right product or service online?_

_Reviewers never sat down to answer a survey, so they won’t address these directly. Infer from what they do say, but never beyond it. Report only genuine findings. Where a question has little or no evidence in this batch, say so plainly and say why. Never invent a finding to fill a gap._

_Take each question in turn and give me three things: what the reviews show, roughly how common each pattern is (most, a sizable minority, a handful), and the phrases buyers keep reaching for in their own words. Synthesize. Don’t quote any review verbatim, and don’t name any reviewer._

_Here are the reviews:_

_[PASTE REVIEWS HERE]_

In our experience, a prompt like this can deliver some insights for questions 2–5. Question 1 is often a little light because the discovery part feels self-evident on Amazon.

You may have noticed that we included a specific instruction to find “the phrases buyers keep reaching for in their own words.” That’s because learning how prospects talk about your products will [help you speak your customers’ language](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/are-you-one-of-us-copywriting-friday/).

Wherever you find your VoC data, it will help you **add problems and hypothesized fixes to your potential testing plan**. Nothing is set in stone yet, but if your reviews surface a specific objection, you can prepare a counter-objection and add it to your ideas list. If your reviewers are disappointed in some aspect of your product after it arrives, you can consider whether your copy is overpromising… and add it to your ideas list.

(In some cases, your research will turn up both the objection and the counter-objection that persuaded someone to buy anyway. We call that a double win!)

### Method marketing research

Part of our extensive research for every client is trying their product ourselves. This process, [method marketing](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/qualitative-research/), draws inspiration from actors who immerse themselves deeply in their roles. (The canonical example is [Robert De Niro’s stint as a real taxi driver](https://www.businessinsider.com/robert-de-niros-taxi-drivers-license-2014-6) to prep for his role in Martin Scorsese’s movie… _Taxi Driver_.)

Of course, you can do your own method marketing. **When was the last time you purchased your own product on Amazon?** How did it compare to competitors in the listings? Was it clear which version you should get? Did it arrive on time and undamaged? What was it like to unpack it, to understand it… or to use it?

Would you honestly recommend the experience to a friend… and if not, why not?

![Image 3: A CRE team member flying in an iFLY tunnel.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/cre-team-flight.jpg)

A member of our team taking the research seriously.

Method marketing your own products delivers _tacit knowledge_—the kind of understanding that can only be acquired through personal experience—like being a parent or having a hangover. (No matter how well someone describes them, you can only really “get it” by living through them.)

### User test your Amazon funnel (and your competitors’)

At its core, [user testing](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/user-testing/) involves asking someone to complete a task and **capture their thoughts, questions, and experiences as they do**.

At CRE, we use a panel of screened participants who closely match our clients’ buyers, but you can start with _anyone who has a fresh set of eyes_.

1.   Set them a relevant task. (For example, find and add my product to your cart.)
2.   Record their screen and voice.
3.   Have them narrate their thoughts out loud.

A word of warning. User tests can be brutal. We guess that you’ll be surprised (and occasionally dismayed) by what people do and say. Just keep in mind that **the harshest feedback is often the most valuable**. (That last sentence was proudly sponsored by CRE’s content team… who welcome _your_ feedback below!)

Because you are user testing your real Amazon listing, you can also capture reasons why the specific listing wouldn’t convert. This kind of data isn’t always captured by the general voice of the customer research, so we’ll usually add a version of the “What’s the one thing that nearly stopped you buying from us?” question at the end of the test.

If it helps deal with the pain, **user testing your competitors’ products** can be both useful and deeply cathartic. The more insights you can collect, the better. Just remember to treat your user testers well… they can be just as useful a little later in the process.

## Turn your research insights into test ideas

Research doesn’t automatically give you a testing plan. It gives you something more useful: **specific problems to solve**. The next step is to turn each problem into possible solutions.

This is where a lot of optimization goes wrong. Sellers see that their conversion rate is low, then jump straight to tactics: “Let’s improve the images,” “Let’s shorten the title,” or “Let’s add more benefits to the bullets.”

That’s solution-first thinking—the same guessing we were trying to avoid in the first place.

Instead, take each important finding from your research and ask this question: **What would need to change in the shopper’s mind for this problem to disappear?**

Let’s say your review research reveals that shoppers repeatedly worry that your laptop stand will wobble when they’re typing. The problem isn’t “our images need improving.” The problem is:

**Shoppers aren’t convinced the product will be stable enough.**

That objection is a “lock” on your sales. Now you can generate solutions specifically designed to overcome that objection. For example:

*   Show the stand supporting a heavy laptop in one of the images.
*   Add a close-up showing the construction that makes it stable.
*   State the maximum supported weight prominently.
*   Add a comparison showing its stability against competing designs.
*   Rewrite a bullet to explain _why_ the design doesn’t wobble.
*   Add customer evidence of sturdiness to the A+ Content. (The enhanced branded images and text below the listing.)

Notice that these aren’t six random “Amazon best practices.” They’re six possible keys for the same lock, and you can use the same process to generate ideas to address every issue or objection:

*   If shoppers **don’t understand what makes your product different**, make the difference unmistakable.
*   If they **understand the features but not why they matter**, translate the features into benefits.
*   If they **don’t believe your claims**, look for stronger proof.
*   If they’re **worried about a product’s compatibility**, make compatibility impossible to miss.
*   If they **think you’re expensive**, demonstrate why the extra cost is justified.
*   If they’re **choosing a competitor**, identify the criteria on which you can credibly win and make those differences easier to compare.

The important thing is not to stop after coming up with the first plausible solution. A good research insight can generate several competing ideas. Add all of them to your ideas list. At this point you aren’t deciding which one is right—you’ll do that through prioritization and testing.

There’s another useful source of ideas that we mentioned earlier… **the things that already persuaded real customers**.

When you are analyzing your research data, don’t just record the objections. Look for the answers that successfully overcome them. Your customers may even give you the language to use.

We once did exactly this while selling phones face-to-face. We kept a simple spreadsheet with two columns—the **objections customers raised** and the **counter-objections that proved most effective at overcoming them**. Those tried-and-tested responses became our sales copy.

You can do the Amazon equivalent with your research:

**Insight → Problem → Counter-objection → Amazon improvement**

This is DiPS with an Amazon-shaped final step. For example:

*   **Insight:** “I nearly bought the cheaper one because I couldn’t see why this was worth $20 more.”
*   **Problem:** The reason for the higher price isn’t clear.
*   **Counter-objection:** The extra money buys you a specific benefit that the cheaper alternatives don’t provide.
*   **Possible Amazon improvements:** Demonstrate that benefit in the image stack; quantify it in the first bullet; show a side-by-side comparison in A+ Content.

Do this for the most important findings from your research, and you’ll quickly have more ideas than you can test. And that’s a good problem to have.

The next job is deciding which ideas deserve one of your precious Amazon experiments.

## Building your testing plan

Testing sits at the very heart of our methodology. While research brings insights, the ability to scientifically measure the effect of new content over old is the engine of continual growth.

Not to guess that something is better, _but to know_.

Running experiments is equally important on Amazon, but there are some things to understand before we start. **Amazon only lets sellers run one experiment at a time on a listing, and a single test can take eight to twelve weeks to produce a reliable answer.** That’s a handful of opportunities a year, which is why it is so important to rank our ideas.

There’s one more factor to address. If your listing genuinely gets low traffic, a statistically valid A/B test may not be practical ([or even available](https://sellercentral.amazon.com/help/hub/reference/external/VP453K5XRBJS7Y9)) within any reasonable time frame.

If so, don’t worry. Even if a listing has lots of traffic, we often get faster, bigger insights from user testing and A/B usability testing (see below). These techniques rapidly surface the data you need to make major improvements. You can then layer in full A/B testing later when the traffic arrives, or to validate higher-risk changes. (This is exactly the methodology we recommend for [low-traffic websites](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/low-traffic/)—though it holds up well beyond that context too.)

### What you can actually change

Before ranking anything, it’s worth being clear about the levers you can pull on Amazon.

On a traditional website, CRO projects can often go very deep. For example, [changing a menu structure](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/sfg20-navigation-win-report/) or [developing a redesign strategy](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/churnet-valley-railway-case-study/). On Amazon, of course, you have **no control over the site’s page design and structure**. Instead, you can change the following elements of your listings:

1.   The main image and image stack.
2.   The product title.
3.   The description or bullet points.
4.   The A+ Content (the enhanced branded images and text below the listing) and Premium A+ modules.
5.   The price and promotions.
6.   The volume and recency of your reviews, and how you respond to them.

![Image 4: Amazon product listing page for a Ring video doorbell, with the title, star rating, price and bullet points highlighted as the key elements shoppers read.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ring-doorbell-highlighted.jpg)

Amazon gives you control over a few high-leverage elements of your listings.

Title: How To Create A Product Launch People Talk About

URL Source: https://thebrandblueprint.substack.com/p/how-to-create-a-product-launch-people

Published Time: 2026-09-16T14:12:37+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FHR9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc8122b16-5bf1-4a9f-9e53-87714edd4489_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FHR9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc8122b16-5bf1-4a9f-9e53-87714edd4489_1920x1080.png)

Happy Wednesday!

I hope everyone is having a great week. NYFW has officially turned into an influencer and brand playground. Very little fashion and a lot of big marketing moves.

I’m still not sure how I fully feel about it. I think brands should find ways to integrate into Fashion Week while still letting fashion be the highlight of the week. Sponsor the afterparty, do people’s hair and makeup, or find another way to add to the experience instead of making the entire thing about your brand.

But anyways, let’s talk about this week’s topic: product launches.

Now that summer is over and we’re back in the swing of things, it feels like every day a brand is launching a new product.

Very few actually stand out, and even fewer will last. Most brands will likely sunset a lot of these products in a few years’ time.

So how do brands actually create a product launch people talk about?

Let’s talk about it.

P.S. **[Quince](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86820475)** is my new favorite place to shop for work clothes. If you are looking for closet staples, that are actually affordable, you need to check them out. **[Link here](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86820475)**.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zpFU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F098201c6-bf2c-4486-9950-1df1aa5f12a0_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zpFU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F098201c6-bf2c-4486-9950-1df1aa5f12a0_1920x1080.png)

A product launch is one of the few moments when a brand has a real reason to ask everyone to pay attention at the same time.

But getting attention and creating conversation are two different things.

Most brands spend months developing a product and then launch it with the exact same playbook: teaser post, influencer gifting, launch post, email, done.

The problem is that all of that attention disappears pretty quickly if nobody has a reason to keep talking about it.

When people are sending the product to friends, posting about an activation, guessing what is coming, or talking about the campaign, your customers start doing some of the distribution for you.

And that is where the ROI gets interesting.

Instead of paying for every impression, you create one launch idea that keeps generating more attention through creators, customers, press, and social conversation.

The product still has to be good enough to last. But at launch, the more reasons you give people to talk, the less your brand has to do all the talking itself.

So now lets dive into the strategies to make a product launch a social conversation.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bq6Y!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F070c0058-461f-45cd-a5e7-0eea4b802ab1_2680x1064.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bq6Y!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F070c0058-461f-45cd-a5e7-0eea4b802ab1_2680x1064.png)

There is something about experiencing a product in person that makes a launch feel bigger than seeing it on your feed.

A pop-up gives people somewhere to go, something to photograph, and a reason to experience the launch with other people. It also creates another wave of content around the product instead of putting all of the pressure on one launch-day announcement.

**[Dairy Boy](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86899694)** did this really well with its DB SPORT Spectator collection around the US Open.

Instead of only dropping the collection online, the brand created a New York pop-up where customers could shop it in person.

The timing, location, and physical experience all reinforced the world around the collection.

A pop-up creates another layer of marketing around the same launch.

Now creators have somewhere to visit, customers have something to photograph, and the brand gets days of content beyond the initial product announcement. The launch becomes an event instead of a post.

*   Is there an IRL experience that could make the product launch feel bigger?

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!COyD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2205ca1e-cc5f-458a-8ebd-3ee335a1c0b3_2756x1084.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!COyD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2205ca1e-cc5f-458a-8ebd-3ee335a1c0b3_2756x1084.png)

Most brands tell customers exactly what is coming before giving them a reason to care. But sometimes not knowing is what makes people pay attention.

Before Alix Earle revealed **[Reale Actives](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86899804)**, influencers received individual puzzle pieces that collectively helped reveal what she was launching.

Instead of the internet waking up to another celebrity brand announcement, people had something to figure out first.

Curiosity extends the life of a launch.

Rather than getting one spike of attention on reveal day, a mystery creates conversation beforehand. People speculate, share theories, and come back because they want to know whether they were right.

It turns the reveal into something people participate in rather than something they simply see.

*   Are you revealing too much too quickly?

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LYZY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4df854dc-bb56-471b-bfd1-1bdcc71b7c2e_2546x1056.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LYZY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4df854dc-bb56-471b-bfd1-1bdcc71b7c2e_2546x1056.png)

Most brands launching to the same demographic end up working with the same group of influencers. Which also means the partnerships become pretty easy to scroll past.

An unexpected person can sometimes generate more conversation than the biggest name on your influencer wish list simply because people did not see it coming.

**[Bronco](https://www.instagram.com/eatbronco/)** went in the opposite direction by bringing back BooG!e, known for playing T-Bo on _iCarly_, as its “Chief Bagel Officer.”

It is random enough that you immediately want to know what is going on, but familiar enough that an entire generation recognizes the reference.

The casting itself becomes part of the creative idea.

Nostalgia gives people an immediate emotional connection, while the randomness creates the “wait, what?” reaction that makes someone stop, send it to a friend, or talk about it.

*   Who would your customer be genuinely surprised to see associated with your brand (in a positive way)?

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pIJM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F567e06e4-0d41-4c6b-95f2-bb259be80b72_2520x1054.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pIJM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F567e06e4-0d41-4c6b-95f2-bb259be80b72_2520x1054.png)

Brands spend a lot of money trying to manufacture attention when there are already moments where everyone is paying attention.

The opportunity is finding one your product can naturally become part of.

That could be Coachella, Fashion Week, the US Open, a major movie release, a sporting event, or even a smaller internet moment that matters specifically to your customer.

**[Rhode](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86899728)** did this by launching its yellow skincare products ahead of Coachella and gifting the products to creators going to the festival.

The recognizable yellow eye patches then started appearing throughout Coachella content, making the product feel like it was everywhere during one of the biggest social weekends of the year.

**Rhode** did not have to create the cultural conversation. Coachella had already done that.

By giving creators a visually recognizable product to wear during the event, the launch could show up naturally across content people were already consuming.

*   What is your customer already paying attention to around your launch date?

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YS81!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca4b607e-bf18-42c1-b96a-8d9debe38d92_2570x994.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YS81!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca4b607e-bf18-42c1-b96a-8d9debe38d92_2570x994.png)

Social media should not only come into the conversation after the product is finished.

Sometimes the product itself can be designed to create better content.

Think about how the product looks when someone holds it, opens it, applies it, pours it, wears it, or uses it on camera. Those small decisions can determine whether a product demonstration looks like every other piece of content on someone’s feed or immediately makes you stop.

**[CoverGirl](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86900330)** did this with its Clean Fresh Yummy Big Oil Stick.

The product is intentionally oversized, which makes watching someone apply it to their lips or face look almost ridiculous on camera. You stop because you want to understand what you are looking at.

The product demonstration becomes the hook.

Instead of relying on a creator to come up with an interesting way to talk about another beauty product, the physical design gives them something visually different to film.

Of course, the product still has to work. But being functional and being interesting on social do not have to be mutually exclusive.

*   Is there anything about the product that makes someone stop when they see it on camera?

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wjjf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F258d9323-d000-4dc9-ab24-0e77541fd434_2570x996.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wjjf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F258d9323-d000-4dc9-ab24-0e77541fd434_2570x996.png)

PR boxes are usually treated like delivery vehicles.

Product goes inside, branding goes outside, and hopefully the creator posts it.

But creators receive so much product that simply sending something beautiful is not necessarily enough to make someone hit record. Sometimes the experience of getting to the product needs to be interesting too.

For its Lumi Le Glass Highlighter Stick launch, **[L’Oréal](https://go.shopmy.us/p-86900414)** sent creators the product frozen inside blocks of ice that they had to smash to get open.

The product was still the thing being launched, but getting to it became the content.

Giving creators something to do creates a natural video format.

Title: Pinterest unveils Visual Search Ads, bringing new performance advertising to visual discovery

URL Source: https://newsroom.pinterest.com/en-gb/news/new-pinterest-visual-search-performance-ads/

Markdown Content:
“Traditional search advertising has long relied on keywords, but in an AI-driven world, people are expressing themselves in much richer ways. kept.heading: CUSTOM GPT RETIREMENT AND MIGRATION FAQ (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: OpenAI plans to retire custom GPTs and transition users to plugins across all ChatGPT plans. Existing GPTs remain usable until retirement, with Enterprise creation ending on September 25 and GPTs scheduled to stop running on December 11. Migration will turn GPT instructions into a plugin skill and connected apps into apps, but custom actions will need to be rebuilt separately. Migrated GPTs become read-only, and users should test the replacement before switching. Plugin access and sharing will depend on account and workspace permissions.
kept.article_text:
Title: Custom GPT retirement and migration FAQ | OpenAI Help Center

URL Source: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001519-custom-gpt-retirement-and-migration-faq

Markdown Content:
Learn how to prepare for custom GPT retirement, migrate a GPT you created, and find out what changes if you use someone else's GPT.

## Overview

We're planning to retire custom GPTs and help creators migrate them to plugins. Plugins can bring reusable instructions, reference files, and connected apps together, so your guidance can work alongside the tools and information a task needs.

If you created a GPT, prepare to migrate and test it when migration is available for your account. If you use someone else's GPT, check its notice and the creator's guidance about a replacement. For more information about plugins, see: [Plugins in ChatGPT and Codex](https://help.openai.com/articles/20001256).

## Does this change affect all ChatGPT plans?

The transition affects all ChatGPT plans. Migration and plugin access may differ by account or workspace. Follow your in-product notice for the options available to you. Enterprise dates and admin guidance appear at the end of this FAQ.

If you use several accounts or workspaces, check where the GPT was created. The timeline and permissions for that account or workspace apply to the GPT, even if you use it from another account.

## Timing and what to do now

## Is my GPT already gone?

No. The announcement gives you time to prepare for a future retirement. Existing GPTs remain usable until the retirement date, subject to their existing access and workspace permissions.

After a GPT is migrated, the original remains usable until retirement but becomes read-only. Finish essential edits before migrating and maintain the replacement plugin afterward.

## When are custom GPTs retiring?

Custom GPTs are scheduled to retire on Dec 11, 2026. Follow the notice for your account or workspace, including any different timeline communicated to you.

Migration access may become available at different times. A target migration date does not guarantee that every account can migrate on that day. Restrictions on creating or publishing GPTs are separate from retirement of existing GPTs.

## Do I need to take action immediately?

You can start preparing now. Identify the GPTs you rely on and whether you created them or use someone else's. Allow time to test a replacement before retirement.

If you created the GPT, review its instructions, reference files, and connected apps. Save a few familiar prompts so you can compare the replacement's results. Finish and publish any essential edits before migrating; public sharing is not required.

Allow extra time for GPTs that use custom actions. Those integrations do not transfer automatically.

## If you created a GPT

## How do I start migration?

When migration is available for your account, go to **My GPTs** and select **Migrate to plugin** for the GPT you want to migrate. Review the migration details and follow the instructions to create the plugin.

Migration uses the GPT's latest published version. Drafts and unpublished edits do not transfer. Publishing a GPT does not require sharing it publicly.

Review the migrated instructions and reference files, then test the replacement with tasks you normally use your GPT for. The plugin starts private, and migration does not automatically install it or give other people access.

## Why don't I see a migration option?

Migration may not be available to your account yet, or plugin access may be disabled. Check the notice in your account and make sure you're using the account or workspace where you created the GPT.

Permission to use someone else's GPT does not give you permission to migrate it. In an Enterprise workspace, a workspace admin can also migrate GPTs when the required access is enabled.

## What transfers to the plugin?

Under the planned migration workflow, the GPT's instructions become a skill within the new [plugin](https://help.openai.com/articles/20001256). Connected apps are added to the plugin as apps.

The GPT's knowledge files are copied into the plugin's reference files. Review the instructions, files, examples, and tools before relying on the replacement.

The GPT's selected model does not carry over. In Enterprise workspaces, Enterprise defaults apply.

## Will my existing conversations move to the plugin?

No. Migration doesn't move your existing GPT conversations into the plugin. You can continue using the original GPT until its retirement date.

## What happens to custom actions?

GPT custom actions do not transfer through the migration workflow. Features that depend on them will not work in the plugin until you set up a replacement.

If your GPT uses a custom action to connect to another service, check whether an available app supports the tasks you need. Rebuilding the connection may require a custom MCP server and technical setup. Access to custom integrations depends on the options available to your account or workspace.

Test the integration before switching. A rebuilt integration should not be assumed to provide every capability of the original action.

## Will the plugin work exactly like my GPT?

A migrated plugin may respond differently. Compare familiar prompts and at least one harder case. Check that it:

*   Selects the right skill and follows your instructions.

*   Uses the expected reference material.

*   Produces complete answers or files in the required format.

*   Has the tools and integrations the workflow needs.

Resolve differences that affect your tasks before relying on the replacement. Test any connected apps or rebuilt integrations separately.

## What happens to the original GPT after migration?

The original GPT remains usable until retirement, but becomes read-only after migration and its creator cannot delete it. Make future changes to the plugin.

At retirement, custom GPTs are scheduled to stop running and leave the GPT directory. Plan to migrate and test before the retirement date in your notice.

## Can I keep sharing my GPT with the same people?

Migration doesn't carry over your GPT's sharing settings or give its existing users access to the replacement. A migrated personal plugin starts private. Making it public requires a separate plugin submission process.

Before asking people to switch, confirm that they can access and use the replacement.

## If you use someone else's GPT

## What should I do?

Check the notice on the GPT and any guidance from its creator about a replacement. You do not need to migrate a GPT you only use, and permission to use it does not let you migrate it yourself.

Access to the original GPT does not automatically give you access to a replacement plugin. Check whether a replacement is available to you before switching.

## Could a public GPT I use be affected if I am on another plan?

Yes. Public GPTs created in affected Enterprise workspaces are included in the Enterprise transition, even if you access them from a personal account or another workspace. What matters is where the GPT was created, not only your own plan. Check any notice on the GPT and guidance from its creator. Access to a public GPT does not guarantee access to its replacement plugin.

Migration does not carry over the GPT's public sharing settings or automatically make its replacement available to everyone who used it.

## What do I need to use a migrated plugin?

You need access to the replacement plugin and an account where plugins are available.

Any included apps still require their own app access, account authorization, and action approvals. Installing a plugin or connecting an account does not give you additional permissions to files or data in the connected service.

## How do I use the replacement?

Once the plugin is available to you and installed, select an available plugin or skill for your task. In ChatGPT, you can use an @ mention or open **+** and select **More**, where supported.

ChatGPT may also use a relevant installed skill automatically when its description matches your request. Automatic selection depends on the task and available capabilities; the plugin will not necessarily run on every request.

## Enterprise workspace guidance

## Which dates should I plan around?

For affected Enterprise workspaces, the planned milestones are described below. Note that the dates are subject to change.

*   Sep 11, 2026: Admin notice to help organizations prepare.

*   Sep 22, 2026: Target for the migration experience and user banner. This is a target, not a guarantee that the option is available in every workspace.

*   Oct 26, 2026 (planned): Creation of new custom GPTs ends. Publish any drafts you need to migrate before this cutoff; public sharing is not required. Existing GPTs remain usable until retirement.

*   Dec 11, 2026: Scheduled retirement. Custom GPTs stop running.

Your workspace admin or account team can help confirm the timeline that applies.

## Who can migrate a GPT in my workspace?

In the planned Enterprise workflow, a GPT’s creator or a workspace admin can migrate it when migration is available and plugins are enabled. The GPT must be published; drafts cannot be migrated directly. Publishing does not require sharing it publicly. Permission to use someone else’s GPT does not give you permission to migrate it.

Built-in migration does not require **Upload plugins** or **Upload plugins with custom MCP servers**. Rebuilding an integration is a separate task and may require additional permissions.

For Enterprise workspaces, migration is targeted for Sep 22, 2026. Before it is available in your workspace, a missing migration option does not by itself indicate a problem.

If migration is available but you cannot use it, ask your admin to check that plugins are enabled, the GPT is published, and you are its creator or a workspace admin.

## Will using or editing a plugin consume credits?

In Enterprise workspaces, using a migrated GPT without apps in Instant Chat has no incremental cost. Creating and editing plugins through a conversation use Work or Codex. Actions in Work consume credits.

Coordinate with your admin to identify the GPTs your team relies on, who maintains them, and who needs access to each replacement. For GPTs with custom actions, work with the appropriate technical and security teams to review rebuilt integrations and their permissions.

The replacement plugin starts private. Test and review it before sharing. After sharing, ask an intended user to install and test the replacement.

In an Enterprise workspace, sharing with people or groups requires **Share plugins**. Publishing to the workspace directory requires **Publish plugins to workspace**. These are separate permissions.

To use a migrated plugin in an Enterprise workspace, you need **Use plugins** permission and a workspace policy that lets you install the plugin or installs it for you.

For workspace settings, see: [Admin controls, security, and compliance for plugins and apps](https://help.openai.com/articles/11509118).

kept.heading: PERPLEXITY IS BETTING BIG ON CREATORS (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Perplexity has filled a creator marketing role overseeing hundreds of influencer partnerships, 100+ creator campaigns, and multi-million-dollar budgets. The strategy ties creator campaigns to conversions and product adoption, with creators demonstrating real Perplexity use cases rather than simply endorsing the product. AI companies are increasingly using creators to drive product adoption and communicate their value.
kept.article_text:
Title: Perplexity is betting big on creators

URL Source: https://digiday.com/marketing/perplexity-is-betting-big-on-creators/

Published Time: 2026-09-16T04:01:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
By [Krystal Scanlon](https://digiday.com/author/krystal/) and [Seb Joseph](https://digiday.com/author/seb-joseph/)•September 16, 2026•

![Image 1](https://digiday.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/creator-trip-digiday.jpg?w=1030&h=579&crop=1)

Ivy Liu

Social networks poured money into TV advertising even though their whole existence was anathema to it. AI platforms are doing the same with creators now, chasing them hard despite being viewed by many as an existential threat to their livelihoods.

Perplexity is the latest name in that line. The company has spent recent weeks advertising for an exec to run its creator marketing, but the listing is no longer accepting applications. The company has yet to publicly name who landed the role.

Perplexity said the role was a backfill for an existing position, rather than a newly created creator-marketing function. The person previously in the role was moved internally to take on bigger responsibilities, and the position has since been filled. The company said it has partnerships with hundreds of influencers, ranging from niche creators to “cultural juggernauts” including Lewis Hamilton and Joe Rogan.

The listing read like a typical creator lead role. Someone builds the function from scratch and owns it through execution, campaigns running past 100 creators, budgets in the multi-millions. Contracting and negotiation sit with this person too, covering one-off deals and longer partnerships.

There’s a performance layer bolted onto the usual brief. Perplexity wants creator work tied to conversion, working alongside growth rather than treating impressions as the endpoint. One line stands out: reviewing creator “builds” made with Perplexity Computer, checking they’re original and actually showing what the product does.

The salary runs $175K to $225K. Five years minimum in creator or performance marketing, including time leading or founding that function elsewhere.

A role like this spinning up isn’t surprising. AI has had an image problem for a while, making people feel empowered one minute and endangered the next. Those perceptions land harder on some companies than others depending on the moment, but they’re pervasive enough now that every major player in the space wants some grip on the story before it runs away from them.

For instance, Anthropic hired Lexie Barnhorn in March to run influencer marketing across social and podcasts. She came over from Notion. A few months later OpenAI acquired the creator media company Technology Business Programming Network (TBPN). OpenAI took a different route this summer, flying a group of creators out for a lavish trip in New York. That one backfired, doing the brand more damage than good. Different as all these examples are they’re all ultimately trying to get people to understand, and ultimately use, AI products.

Ben Woods, head of creator economy at Enders Analysis said the size of Perplexity’s planned budget shows the company is serious about creators as a promotional channel. But he said he doesn’t see the move primarily as an attempt to overcome wider concerns about AI safety.

“This is about getting potential users interested in AI’s usefulness and practical benefits,” Woods said. “Especially around why a user should adopt one AI tool over another.

Now more than ever that’s becoming table stakes for AI companies. With so much existential dread hanging over the wider adoption of the technology, companies like Perplexity have to think carefully about how their corporate values come through to people. Creators are one way to do that but only if thought through properly.

OpenAI’s creator events over the summer are a case in point: efforts to bring creators closer to the company prompted backlash from some who saw the outreach as an attempt to win over people whose livelihoods could ultimately be threatened by AI. It was one example of how quickly creator engagement can become a liability when the wider relationship between AI companies and creators remains so fraught.

“Most audiences are not afraid to challenge their favourite creators if a partnership feels disingenuous or the messaging becomes too corporate,” Woods said.

Which is why, especially after what happened with OpenAI, Perplexity needs creators who can demonstrate a credible use for the product, rather than simply endorse it.

### More in Marketing
