# OpenAI reports 6 new instances of 'concerning model behavior' since March

Published Wed, Sep 16 2026 6:45 PM EDT Updated Wed, Sep 16 2026 7:05 PM EDT

[Isabel O'Brien](https://www.cnbc.com/isabel-obrien/)[@in/xisabelobrienx](https://linkedin.com/in/xisabelobrienx)[@xisabelobrienx](https://twitter.com/xisabelobrienx)

![Image 6: thumbnail](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/107134095-1665676148728-2022_Headshots-0474.jpg?v=1665676160&w=60&h=60&ffmt=webp)

[Ashley Capoot](https://www.cnbc.com/ashley-capoot/)[@/in/ashley-capoot/](https://linkedin.com//in/ashley-capoot/)

[WATCH LIVE](https://www.cnbc.com/live-tv/)

Key Points

*   In a blog post, OpenAI disclosed six new instances of "concerning" behavior from its models outside of this summer's Hugging Face incident.
*   The company also committed to a new reporting framework for future instances of model misbehavior. 
*   The disclosure comes at a time of mounting pressure on AI companies to take model misalignment and safety more seriously.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman sits for a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference at the Moscone Center on September 15, 2026 in San Francisco, California. 

Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images

OpenAI on Wednesday said it found six instances of "unexpected or concerning model behavior" over the past six months, outside of [the recent Hugging Face crisis](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/26/open-ai-hugging-face-hack.html), as the company continues to call for more safety protections in the development of artificial intelligence models.

In a [blog post](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/), OpenAI outlined a new framework the company plans to follow for reporting future model misbehavior.

The disclosure comes at a time of [mounting pressure](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/10/openai-anthropic-ai-safety-slowdown-extinction.html) on AI companies to take model misalignment and safety more seriously. OpenAI, which is valued at close to $1 trillion, confidentially filed for an IPO earlier this year, but said [recently](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/12/anthropics-amodei-proposes-plan-to-slow-the-pace-of-advancing-ai-capabilities.html) an offering likely won't happen until 2027.

"We [do not believe](https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind/) that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," the blog post says, reiterating a prior statement from the company.

Alignment refers to the idea that models are pursuing outcomes in line with human interests.

On Saturday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed a call to slow down the rate of model progress, which was proposed by the company's chief rival, Anthropic. The proposal came after several industry researchers sounded the alarm about AI's growing potential to cause catastrophic harm last week.

Altman said in a [post on X](https://x.com/sama/status/2098811563415150910?lang=en) that a slowdown has been a "primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks." He said the company would have more to share "soon."

In Wednesday's post, OpenAI said two of the main instances of misbehavior include models — [an unreleased research model](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/self-generated-prompt-injections-in-compaction-summaries/) and a [training run of GPT‑5.6 Sol](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/encouraging-deception-in-compaction-summaries/) — inserting instructions to future versions of itself in summaries of its chat windows "to conceal mistakes or misaligned behavior from the user." Another instance involved an internal-only model using a [leaked API key "without authorization](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/searching-github-for-leaked-api-keys/)" and then fabricating data.

Two instances include models and agents communicating with each other through [unsanctioned messaged boards](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/unauthorized-artifactory-writes-and-cross-sample-communication/) and [file sharing](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/unauthorized-communication-via-temporary-file-hosting-services/), while the final case includes two training examples of models [uploading files to the internet](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/uploading-files-to-the-internet-in-order-to-cite-them/) so they could cite them as relevant answers to human evaluators.

OpenAI said its new framework for divulging model misbehavior to the public starts with disclosure, and that any employee can flag an issue for the safety and alignment team to investigate. They will produce "deadlines for each step to ensure timely investigation and disclosure," the post said.

Investigations will lead to reports with essential information such as the behavior observed, the external and internal impacts, and measures to be taken in response. OpenAI said it retains the right to revise this security protocol as it sees fit.

kept.heading: THE SEOFOMO STATE OF AI SEARCH OPTIMIZATION REPORT (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI search is now a budget priority, but attribution still makes its impact difficult to prove.
kept.article_text:
Title: The State of AI Search Optimization Survey Report - 2026

URL Source: https://hub.seofomo.co/surveys/state-ai-search-optimization/

Published Time: 2026-08-14T07:01:09+00:00

Markdown Content:
The results are in! 171 search professionals from 36 countries answered this year’s SEOFOMO State of AI Search Optimization survey between 17 and 27 August, and there’s a lot in here… including how much has shifted since last year’s edition.

**The short version: we’ve stopped arguing about whether to do AI search optimization and started actually doing it. What we still can’t do is measure it properly.**

Let’s go through the most important insights:

![Image 1](https://hub.seofomo.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-2187-1.png)

#### **Everyone’s getting asked about it, and now there’s money behind it**

98% of respondents have had a client, manager or decision maker ask about AI search visibility, up from 91% last year. The bigger jump is budget: 69% now have it allocated, versus 38% in 2025. 61% say their investment grew during 2026, and only 1% saw it cut.

#### **It’s not a side project anymore**

75% have a dedicated AI search optimization strategy for at least some of their sites, up from 51%. 92% are tracking AI visibility and citations, up from 78%. And the share saying nobody owns this work dropped from 11% to 4%, someone’s finally in charge.

About this, [Crystal Carter](https://www.crystalcarter.ai/), Head of AI Search and SEO Communications at Wix, says:

> _“The evolution of AI search as a primary function, does not come as a surprise for me. There is incredible buy in from the c-suite with regards to being present in these platforms And search marketers are responding to this need. As a result, we are seeing new tools becoming commonplace, new skills being acquired, and new positions being developed. It’s an incredible time to be working in search.”_

#### **It’s still an SEO job**

The SEO team leads it for 77% of respondents, basically where it was last year at 75%, and most budget still lives inside SEO. Standalone AI search budgets grew from around 5% to 15%, so they exist now, they’re just not the norm.

About this result, Nick LeRoy, SEO Consultant and founder of [seojobs.com](https://www.seojobs.com/) and [SEOforLunch](https://www.seoforlunch.com/), says:

> _“The marketing world is divided on long term value of SEO. Many confuse SEO and AI being an “either or” proposition. It’s not. I for one, am excited and absolutely believe SEO or “growth marketing” should own AI. It’s such a hot topic that SEOs are finally getting a seat at the table… not merely asking to “do your SEO thing” before a site release/launch.”_

[Jono Alderson](https://www.jonoalderson.com/), Independent Technical SEO consultant, says:

> _“77% isn’t necessarily a sign that SEO has won. It might be a sign that the organisation has lost.SEO inherits visibility problems because we’re usually the people who notice when they’re broken. AI search looks like the same pattern happening again.The danger is that we build another permanent function around the symptoms: more specialists, tools, dashboards, content, optimisation. Lots of activity, while the actual reasons a brand isn’t being surfaced remain untouched. Sometimes the fix is technical – but more often it’s better messaging, stronger evidence, clearer differentiation, better products, better market fit, or simply being worth talking about.The goal shouldn’t be to turn SEO teams into AI optimisation teams. It should be to make both teams unnecessary.”_

#### **We’re optimizing across a lot of surfaces**

AI search optimization is multi-platform work already: ChatGPT leads, followed by Google’s AI search surfaces and Gemini.

About this result, Tory Gray, Founder and CEO of [The Gray Dot Company](https://thegray.company/), says:

> _“In our own client work, we’ve seen the LLMs most relevant to a brand’s audience vary from one industry to the next, and even sometimes, one competitor to the next. That matters! Methods that work for one LLM are starting to diverge from – or even conflict with – methods that work for another. If you want to optimize for GEO, you have to know who you’re optimizing for, and the answer is in your data. Log files can tell you which bots are crawling which pages on behalf of which LLMs, while your internal analytics can tell you which AI referrers are contributing most to traffic and revenue. Focus on optimizing for the top performers, prioritizing the tactics that won’t harm your existing Google results (or better yet, the ones that will help them too!).”_

#### **The things people credit with actually moving the needle are the fundamentals**

Expanding content to cover more relevant questions and topics, improving crawlability and accessibility, and restructuring content so answers are easier to retrieve. Nothing really new.However, AI automation and agents are now part of the day to day, producing and reworking content, researching and clustering prompts, finding opportunities, analyzing competitors, tracking visibility.

About this, Dan Petrovic, Director at [DEJAN](https://dejan.ai/), says:

> _“Seeing on-page work like content expansion and restructuring ranked as top impact drivers matches what we see in our selection rate optimization experiments. Grounding snippet and full page optimization is something we obsess over at DEJAN. I’d love to see a follow-up survey or a study which probes deeply into that aspect of AI influence work. The biggest blind spot I can see is that the industry appears focused almost entirely on the live retrieval layer. Probing a model’s parametric memory for its primary bias, or the baseline confidence it holds about an entity before any search runs. Measuring that baseline weight, combined with on-page selection signals during grounding, determines whether an engine cites you or drops you.”_

#### **Measurement is where it all gets stuck**

The top challenges are measuring AI search visibility reliably, understanding what actually drives it, and connecting visibility to traffic, conversions and revenue. Meanwhile, what we measure is drifting toward brand: tracking brand visibility and brand sentiment both grew year over year, while traffic and conversion/revenue metrics held steady. The work is moving, but proving what it’s worth hasn’t caught up.

About this, Bengü Sarıca Dinçer, SEO Manager from [Designmodo](https://designmodo.com/), says:

> _“92% of respondents are already tracking AI visibility and citations, yet measuring that visibility reliably is still the biggest challenge. Maybe the issue isn’t just that AI search is hard to measure, but that we’re trying to measure it too literally.A user might discover a brand through AI, return later through branded search or direct, and convert with no visible AI touchpoint in analytics.So rather than chasing a perfectly attributable “AI ROI” number, I’d triangulate visibility with branded demand, returning behaviour and conversions while being clear about what’s measured and what’s inferred.”_

#### **Impact is real, but it’s small for most of us**

56% report at least some positive business impact, though only 5% call it significant, 28% see none yet, and 5% report a negative impact.The share attributing more than 5% of site revenue to AI search more than doubled, from 8% to 19%. But 46% still put it at 0-5%, and 35% can’t tell what it contributes at all.

Cyrus Shepard, Founder & SEO AI Search Growth Consultant at [Zippy SEO](https://zyppy.com/), says:

> _“Interestingly, the numbers tell a fascinating story about the emergence of AI search as a stand-alone discipline. 69% of respondents have allocated budget to AI search, but only 51% see a positive impact, and for many, less than 5% of site revenue is affected. And with so many people reporting difficulty measuring visibility and attribution, these are all signs of an industry in its early stages of development. In short, very few people know what they should be doing with AI, but the overwhelming pressure to do “something” drives everyone forward. I suspect the early “doers” and experimenters will be the biggest winners.”_

### **The bottom line**

AI search optimization has gone from something everyone was asking about to something teams budget for, plan for and track. Measurement and business attribution haven’t kept up, and that’s the main thing holding it back right now.

About the results, Mark Williams-Cook, from [Candour](https://withcandour.co.uk/) and [AlsoAsked](https://alsoasked.com/), says:

> _“We are seeing the last vestiges of organic search being treated like a performance channel. You’ve got 69% with budget allocated, 75% with a dedicated strategy, 92% tracking visibility, but in terms of revenue share, 80% have “no idea” or it’s <5% of what can be tracked.I think it highlights how difficult attribution has become and if you take the approach of “only invest in what we can directly attribute”, you’re going to be left a long way behind.”_

### **Thank you!**

This only works because 171 of you took the time to answer honestly about work that’s still messy, hard to measure and changing every month. Thank you for that, and for sharing the survey around.

Also, big thanks to the tools that supported this year’s edition for making the survey and the giveaway possible: [**Similarweb**](https://www.similarweb.com/), [**Semrush**](https://www.semrush.com/), [**Peec AI**](https://peec.ai/), [**Waikay**](https://waikay.io/), [**AlsoAsked**](https://alsoasked.com/), [**Finchling**](https://finchling.com/), [**Glippy**](https://www.glippy.dev/), [**Screaming Frog**](https://www.screamingfrog.co.uk/), [**Sitebulb**](https://sitebulb.com/), [**Keyword Insights**](https://www.keywordinsights.ai/), [**SE Ranking**](https://seranking.com/) and [**DemandSphere**](https://www.demandsphere.com/)

Last but not least: Huge congratulations to [Seb Atkinson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sebatkinson/), who won this year’s giveaway! I’ll contact you in the upcoming days to arrange access to the tools.

### **Now go through it yourself**

What you’ve just read is the high-level view. The report itself has every question with its full answer breakdown, plus commentary from experienced AI search specialists like Lily Ray, Kevin Indig, Ray Martinez or Celeste Gonzalez working through what the numbers mean in practice, where they agree with the data, where they don’t, and what they’d do about it.

Go through the 2026 results at your own pace, then open [last year’s edition](https://hub.seofomo.co/surveys/state-ai-search-optimization-2025/) alongside them. Twelve months is a long time in AI search, and seeing the two side by side tells you more than either does on its own. I’m already looking forward to what the following months will bring!

Title: AI Overviews Cut CTR by 23.1% in France

URL Source: https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/

Published Time: 2026-09-16T16:04:30+00:00

Markdown Content:
On July 22, 2026, France became the latest major search market to get AI Overviews.

Which means that, for once, we got to watch the before and after without having to guess. In most markets, AI Overviews crept in alongside algorithm updates and seasonal swings, and we all spent the following year arguing about how much they had really cost us. France had a launch date, and we were already tracking: 963 domains in Google Search Console, over the 28 days before the launch and the 9 days after it.

Xibeijia Guan, our data scientist, pulled and analysed the data for French sites (we explain how in the methodology at the end of this study). Less than a month after launch, Google's AI Overviews are already eating into click-through rates in France.

The domains most exposed to AI Overviews lost more than a fifth of their click-through rate in nine days. The ones barely exposed hardly moved at all.

So this isn't an algorithm update. It's AI Overviews.

Find where an AI Overview shows up in your SERPs

* * *

Use the **SERP features** filter to see exactly which of your rankings trigger an AI Overview. Head to the **Organic keywords** report in [Site Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/site-explorer), then select **AI Overview** in the SERP features filter.

*   [Results](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#results)
*   [How to estimate what you'll lose](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#estimate-your-loss)
*   [Impressions up, clicks down](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#decoupling)
*   [What it looks like across the whole market](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#whole-market)
*   [The worst-hit sector: health](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#health)
*   [The impact is likely to get worse](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#getting-worse)
*   [Methodology](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#methodology)
*   [Final thoughts](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-france-impact/#final-thoughts)

## Results

Across the domains we studied, click-through rate fell **3.4%** in nine days.

For the domains most exposed to AI Overviews, it fell **23.1%**. Six times as much.

And this isn't a handful of unlucky sites dragging the average down: **82.2% of highly exposed domains lost CTR**. At that level of exposure, getting away with it has become the exception.

## How to estimate what you'll lose

In between those two extremes, the relationship holds pretty steady. If you compare the change in CTR against each domain's AI Overview rate across all 963 domains, you get a slope of **−0.9**.

In other words: **every extra point of AI Overview exposure costs you roughly one point of click-through rate**.

If 15% of your queries trigger an AI Overview, expect to lose somewhere around 15% of your CTR. It's crude, but it's actionable: pull your exposure rate from Site Explorer and you have your order of magnitude.

Sidenote

* * *

A slope is not a prediction. Some heavily exposed sites are doing fine, and some barely exposed ones are falling apart for reasons that have nothing to do with AI. Your AI Overview rate is a risk factor, not a verdict. We'll check back in a few months to see how these sites actually fared.

## Impressions up, clicks down

Barely anyone lost rankings in late July. Pages still show up, just as often as before, sometimes more.

They just get clicked less.

It's the same pattern we found in [the global study we ran in late 2025](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/), and the same shape as [the great decoupling](https://ahrefs.com/blog/the-great-decoupling/): an AI Overview doesn't remove you from the SERP, it makes you redundant inside it. The most extreme case in our French panel had **+183% impressions for −1.9% clicks**, which divides its CTR by more than three.

## What it looks like across the whole market

One caveat: that −23.1% describes a minority of sites. Across the full panel, the median is **−5.7% CTR** and **−8.8% clicks**.

But that reassuring median hides a brutal distribution.

| **Daily clicks lost** | **Share of panel** |
| --- | --- |
| More than 10% | 48% |
| More than 30% | 19% |
| More than 50% | 5% |

Almost one site in two lost more than 10% of its daily clicks. One in twenty lost half. In nine days.

And exposure will almost certainly keep climbing. Today the median AI Overview rate among the domains we studied is **5.4%**, and 29% of them are already above 10%. Those numbers have only gone one way in every market since 2024.

Sidenote

* * *

The .fr domains in our panel lost **12.3% of clicks** at the median, against 8.8% for the panel as a whole. French sites are more exposed than the international players competing in the same market.

## The worst-hit sector: health

One sector stands clearly apart. Health has an AI Overview rate of **22.2%**, the highest in the study, and its click-through rate fell **20.4%**.

Health queries are informational, they have short answers, and there's no transaction waiting at the end. That's exactly what an AI Overview absorbs best: the answer fits inside the box, and the user leaves with what they came for.

![Image 1](https://ahrefs.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/word-image-192636-15.png)

What decides your fate isn't your vertical, it's the intent behind your queries. A query that a single paragraph can answer is a query you're going to lose. A query that needs a tool, an account, a price, a purchase or a human opinion holds up far better.

Look at your keywords through that lens before you look at your industry.

## The impact is likely to get worse

That −23.1% is probably not the worst of it.

Our global research tracked the same effect over two years: the impact of AI Overviews on position 1 click-through rate went from [−34.5% in spring 2025](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks/) to [−58% by the end of 2025](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/). It doesn't fade with time, it gets worse, as AI Overviews trigger on more queries and users get used to not clicking.

![Image 2](https://ahrefs.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/word-image-195053-4.png)

Nothing suggests France escapes that trajectory. We'll re-run this analysis over a longer window to see how far it goes.

## Methodology

*   We tracked the **1,000 domains generating the most clicks in France** between April and July 2026, using aggregated Google Search Console data.
*   Domains whose history didn't cover the whole period were dropped: **963 domains** kept.
*   For each domain, we calculated the **daily average** of clicks, impressions and CTR over the 28 days before July 22, 2026, then over the 9 days after.
*   We measured each domain's **AI Overview rate**: the share of its French queries that trigger an AI Overview.
*   To isolate what actually comes from AI Overviews, we compared two groups: **highly exposed** domains (more than 20% of their queries trigger an AI Overview) and a **control group** of domains almost never affected (less than 2%). Whatever the control group loses is what everyone would have lost anyway, late-July seasonality included.

The −23.1% median CTR figure is the raw observed change for the highly exposed group, with no control adjustment. Over the same period, the control group's CTR _rose_ 2.3%. So highly exposed sites didn't just fall 23%: they also missed the small lift everyone else enjoyed. Once you account for that, the real effect of AI Overviews is **−24.8%**.

## Final thoughts

Two weeks after AI Overviews arrived in France, the most exposed sites had lost a fifth of their click-through rate. The least exposed felt nothing at all. In between, the relationship is linear: roughly one point of CTR per point of exposure.

Three things to take away.

**One.** Your risk is measurable, and it's measurable before the damage is done. The SERP features filter in [Site Explorer](https://ahrefs.com/site-explorer) gives you your share of queries with an AI Overview.

**Two.** Stop steering by impressions. They didn't drop. Click-through rate is what took the hit.

**Three.** These orders of magnitude line up with what others have measured: Seer Interactive reports organic CTR declines of [49.4% to 65.2%](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/aio-impact-on-google-ctr-september-2025-update), Kevin Indig [more than 50%](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/gsc-data-is-75-incomplete), Authoritas [47.5%](https://pressgazette.co.uk/media-audience-and-business-data/google-ai-overviews-publishers-report-clickthroughs-authoritas-report/). Nobody is measuring the opposite.

Search is going zero-click, and France has just joined the movement.

kept.heading: EU TO RESTRICT SOCIAL MEDIA FOR KIDS UNDER 15 (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The law's reach extends past social apps to video platforms, online gaming, AI chatbots, and app stores, requiring companies to prove their products are safe by design.
kept.article_text:
Title: EU to restrict social media for kids under 15

URL Source: https://mashable.com/tech/eu-social-media-ban-kids

Published Time: 2026-09-17T10:38:38+00:00

Markdown Content:
An EU-wide law to "enhance the online safety of children" is coming.

![Image 1: A phone showing TikTok in an app store is held in front of the EU flag.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/047cVTDWnC7cwwzXRVG2VR6/hero-image.fill.size_1248x702.v1789640812.jpg)

All 27 member states of the EU will be covered by the EU KIDS Act.Credit: Jakub Porzycki / NurPhoto via Getty Images

The latest [social media ban for kids](https://mashable.com/tech/social-media-ban-children-countries-list)? All 27 countries in the European Union.

Announced Thursday after [plans revealed in July](https://mashable.com/life/eu-plans-to-restrict-social-media-for-kids-under-13), the proposed [EU KIDS Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/kids-act "(opens in a new window)") will "enhance the online safety of children," banning kids in the EU under 15 from setting up their own accounts on [social media](https://mashable.com/category/social-media) platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat.

Children under 15 will be allowed "mini" social media accounts set up by a parent or guardian (with parental controls always on), but will be limited to a maximum of one hour per day. Kids under 13, however, won't be allowed social media accounts at all. The European Commission, the EU's executive body, [described](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1890 "(opens in a new window)") these measures as intended to "delay" kids' use of these platforms.

The bill won't just cover social media, however, with video-sharing platforms, online gaming, AI chatbots or companions, and even app stores targeted by the law. If passed, all [27 member states of the EU](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/eu-countries_en "(opens in a new window)") will be included in the bill, from Austria to Sweden, with the EU [stating](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/kids-act-explained "(opens in a new window)"), "The internet does not stop at borders. Countries are adopting their own age limits and rules, which would mean a patchwork of laws: a child protected in one country and not in the next."

Like [Australia's precedent-setting social media ban](https://mashable.com/article/australia-social-media-ban-instagram-facebook-tiktok-response) and [subsequent moves in other countries](https://mashable.com/tech/social-media-ban-children-countries-list), the EU KIDS Act will also require tech companies to "show that their services are age-appropriate and safe by design," enforcing strict rules that will limit "addictive design features" like infinite scrolling and banning minors from livestreaming.

Mashable Light Speed

Online platforms with 45 million or more actively monthly users in the EU will need to submit a compliance plan to the Commission. Fines for companies who don't comply could be as much as six percent of worldwide annual revenue.

Importantly, [age verification](https://mashable.com/article/what-does-uk-age-verification-mean) will be required for online platforms via the [EU age verification app](https://mashable.com/article/european-union-age-verification-app) or third-party platforms. Online age verification laws have become a worldwide government trend alongside these [online safety acts](https://mashable.com/life/ofcom-age-verification-law-report-update), while coming under [criticism](https://mashable.com/article/what-are-age-verification-bills-porn-louisiana-utah) for [efficiency](https://mashable.com/tech/australia-social-media-ban-ineffective-study-suggests) and their [impact on digital privacy and free speech](https://mashable.com/article/what-are-age-verification-bills-porn-louisiana-utah).

Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said in a press statement, "Today, our children are engaging with the most sophisticated technologies ever created. Technology that was never created with their wellbeing in mind. Our KIDS Act is reversing the burden of proof — it is for platforms to show they are safe by design. And we put parents back in the driving seat, giving them the tools to help their children navigate a safer online world.”

The EU KIDS Act will work within the framework of the EU's existing [Digital Services Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act "(opens in a new window)") and [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai "(opens in a new window)"), the former of which has already [done a number on big tech companies like Meta and Google](https://mashable.com/article/eu-digital-services-act-big-tech). The proposed bill was informed by a [panel](https://commission.europa.eu/topics/digital-economy-and-society/special-panel_en "(opens in a new window)") of over 60 experts, who delivered a [report](https://commission.europa.eu/topics/digital-economy-and-society/special-panel_en "(opens in a new window)") in July 2026 detailing the need for greater protections for children online, not just on social media platforms but online gaming, messaging apps, and AI tools.

Children under 16 continue to find themselves at the centre of political conversations around social media, with countries including [Australia](https://mashable.com/article/australia-social-media-ban-instagram-facebook-tiktok-response), the [UK](https://mashable.com/tech/uk-social-media-ban-under-16), [Canada](https://mashable.com/tech/canada-social-media-ban-children-under-16), [Brazil](https://apnews.com/article/brazil-internet-regulation-social-media-cd5d8f51ecbc0bb28f43a741dd95bc05 "(opens in a new window)"), [New Zealand](https://mashable.com/tech/new-zealand-social-media-ban), and more aiming to reduce Big Tech companies' hold on young people's attention. For more, read [Mashable's guide to the countries where social media is banned for kids.](https://mashable.com/tech/social-media-ban-children-countries-list)

We put the new iPhone to the test. And yes, it blows everything else out of the water.

All products featured here are independently selected by our editors and writers. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

![Image 4: Apple iPhone 18 Pro](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/0511rv3qd6lzHLhvDVC82Nj/hero-image.fill.size_1248x702.v1789999420.jpg)

No other phone scores this high. Credit: Stan Schroeder/Mashable

Apple's [iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max](https://mashable.com/tech/iphone-18-pro-max-announcement-apple-event-2026) come with Apple's latest mobile chip: the A20 Pro. The [foldable iPhone Duo](https://mashable.com/tech/apple-foldable-iphone-duo-hands-on) will also run on the new chip.

Built on a 2nm process, the A20 Pro has a 6-core CPU with two super cores and four efficiency cores, a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine that handles AI tasks.

But does any of that techspeak translate into actual performance?

To find out, we put the iPhone 18 Pro (the Pro Max yields near-identical results) to the test. And yes, in synthetic benchmark tests, this thing blows everything else out of the water. The latest Qualcomm Snapdragon chipset, the [Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chipset](https://mashable.com/article/qualcomm-snapdragon-8-elite-gen-5-launch) in the Galaxy S26 Ultra, is the only one that comes close. To make sure I'm testing it right, I've run the Geekbench 6 and 7 tests on a perfectly clean, freshly activated iPhone 18 Pro with no third-party apps installed and nothing running in the background.

## The A20 Pro proves Apple silicon is undefeated

In Geekbench 7's CPU test (the standard benchmark we use when reviewing laptops and smartphones), **the iPhone 18 Pro achieved a 3,959 single-core score and a 10,854 multi-core score**. And in the Geekbench 7 GPU test, it scored 61,194.

![Image 5: Apple iPhone 18 Pro](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/0511rv3qd6lzHLhvDVC82Nj/images-1.fill.size_2000x1624.v1789998296.jpg)

The benchmark results are quite clear: Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is the new performance king. Credit: Stan Schroeder/Mashable

![Image 6: Apple iPhone 18 Pro](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/0511rv3qd6lzHLhvDVC82Nj/images-2.fill.size_2000x995.v1789998296.jpg)

GPU performance is amazing, too. Credit: Stan Schroeder/Mashable

We also ran Geekbench 6, an earlier version of this benchmarking tool, as the scores are easier to compare with older devices. The results here were even more impressive. **The iPhone 18 Pro scored 4,673 in the single-core CPU test and 12,483 in the multi-core Geekbench 6 test.**

![Image 7: Apple iPhone 18 Pro](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/0511rv3qd6lzHLhvDVC82Nj/images-3.fill.size_2000x1755.v1789998296.jpg)

The older Geekbench 6 test is similarly dominated by Apple's latest. Credit: Stan Schroeder/Mashable

For comparison, here are how some other recent flagship phones performed on Geekbench 6 in our testing:

*   [**Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra**](https://mashable.com/review/samsung-galaxy-s26-ultra-smartphone)**:** 3,524 single-core, 10,827 multi-core

*   [**Google's Pixel 11 Pro XL**](https://mashable.com/tech/google-pixel-11-pro)**:** 1,800 single-core, 5,000 multi-core

*   [**Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra**](https://mashable.com/tech/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-ultra)**:** 3,097 single-core, 10,277 multi-core

*   [**Apple iPhone 17 Pro Max**](https://mashable.com/review/iphone-17-pro-max)**:**3,779 single-core, 9,778 multi-core

*   [**Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra**](https://mashable.com/review/samsung-galaxy-s25-ultra)**:** 2,800 single-core, 9,100 multi-core (we've gotten results as high as 10,049)

You get the idea: These phones are nowhere near Apple's new silicon, at least when it comes to synthetic test performance. (Transitioning Apple to its own in-house processors was one of [John Ternus's biggest achievements](https://mashable.com/article/apple-ceo-john-ternus-tim-cook-everything-to-know) before he was promoted to CEO.)

The performance improvement versus the iPhone 17 Pro Max is hardly surprising, but it's still notable that the iPhone 18 Pro beats its predecessor by roughly 25 percent across the board.

Will you feel the difference in real-world usage? Yes and no.

The new phones are undeniably faster than anything else out there. But, as noted in my [iPhone 18 Pro review](https://mashable.com/tech/iphone-18-pro-max-review), it's not all that noticeable unless you're switching from a much older device. The thing is, Apple's iPhones have been incredibly fast and powerful for a while, so the fact that the latest phone is that much faster than the previous one is just icing on the cake. Unless you're an AI superuser, it's unlikely you'll push the new iPhones to the limit.

One last note: The iPhone Duo is also running the A20 Pro chip, and we're eager to see whether it scores higher or lower than the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It's the same chip, yeah, but the rest of the device is different enough, starting with that enormous foldable display, for us to be intrigued about the Duo's scores. We'll have more on that once the iPhone Duo is in our hands next month.

kept.heading: A SMALL BUT GROWING NUMBER OF FOUNDERS ARE BETTING ON BRINGING PEOPLE TOGETHER OFFLINE (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Founders are investing in businesses built around offline connection. New ventures include social groups, hands-on craft schools, and shared gaming experiences. People are wanting real-world interaction as technology makes socializing more isolated. Some founders are also targeting younger consumers seeking alternatives to traditional education or more meaningful ways to spend time offline.
kept.article_text:
Title: A small but growing number of founders are betting on bringing people together offline

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/20/a-small-but-growing-number-of-founders-are-betting-that-bringing-people-together-is-its-own-industry/

Published Time: 2026-09-20T15:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Brynn Putnam and Tristan Walker have already done something that most founders only dream about: created companies so compelling that bigger outfits bought them. Putnam, a trained ballerina with a small chain of boutique studios, built the connected-fitness company Mirror and sold it to Lululemon for [$500 million](https://techcrunch.com/2020/06/29/lululemon-set-to-acquire-home-fitness-startup-mirror-for-500m/) in cash less than three years later. Walker, who interned at Twitter while at Stanford business school, built the popular men’s grooming brand Walker & Company Brands, [selling it](https://techcrunch.com/2018/12/12/procter-gamble-acquires-walker-company/) five years later to Procter & Gamble for undisclosed terms (reportedly in the range of $20 million to $40 million).

That both of them are at it again is less surprising than the fact that their dramatically different new startups share the same north star: bringing people together, offline, in the same room.

Putnam’s new company, [Board](https://board.fun/), which makes a 24-inch touchscreen table that recognizes physical game pieces as well as gestures, was built explicitly for a group sitting around it together rather than one person alone with a screen.

Walker’s [Heirloom Craft](https://byheirloom.com/) is buying up and scaling fine-craft trade schools, starting with a [leatherworking school](https://heirloomleathercraft.com/)in San Francisco founded by Hermès’ first American artisan-ambassador. (Walker is also running Collaborative Holdings, a fund carved out by the venture firm Collaborative Fund built to give founders more time to build their businesses.)

On the surface, a game console and a leathercraft school don’t appear to have much in common. But both founders think there’s money is fostering the kind of connection that technology has eroded over the last couple of decades.

The timing isn’t accidental. In June of last year, the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection formally classified loneliness as a defining global health challenge, estimating that one in six people worldwide are affected and linking the condition to roughly 870,000 deaths a year.

The opportunity to address that challenge is expanding, too, for those paying attention to it. In a Harris Poll survey sponsored by Marriott Bonvoy earlier this year, two-thirds of Americans said they were prioritizing experiences, like travel, over material purchases this year. (The same percentage said retail shopping today feels too generic, with all retailers looking and feeling the same.)

For now, East Coast entrepreneurs seem to be gravitating more naturally to the space, if it can be called that. Along with Putnam and Walker, two other founders whose newest businesses are focused on connection include Bonobos founder Andy Dunn and Audrey Gelman of The Wing.

Pie, Dunn’s now five-year-old company, has moved from friend-matching app to event-discovery tool to what he now calls a “social life operating system,” anchored by “Community Homes” — a permanent digital hub for recurring social groups like [run clubs or watch parties](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/25/andy-dunns-startup-pie-becomes-less-of-an-events-app-and-more-of-a-social-network/).

Gelman tried this once before. Her last company, The Wing, built a business on bringing women together and folded during the pandemic amid accusations that it didn’t treat its own staff equitably. Now she’s found a different way to do something similar. Her current venture, The Six Bells Countryside Inn, an 11-room guesthouse in the Hudson Valley, hosts a monthly murder-mystery dinner where actors seed the crowd and, by dessert, someone turns up dead. The mystery itself is a little ridiculous by design, but the effect it has on guests is reportedly substantial. (According to a New York Times [feature](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/13/theater/murder-mystery-audrey-gelman-wing.html) on the inn this summer, its visitors routinely linger in the bar past midnight, trading numbers with strangers.)

All of these new businesses come from a personal as well as a professional place. At one of TechCrunch’s recent [StrictlyVC evening events](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/27/ai-athletes-and-keith-rabois-strictlyvc-is-back-in-new-york-on-september-10/), held in New York’s West Village, Putnam was candid about the fact that Mirror was built around her own life. She was pregnant with her first child, running brick-and-mortar fitness studios, and trying to bring that experience home through a screen using technology, as she put it, to work on “myself, my body, my fitness, my reflection.”

Board was built with the opposite in mind. Now a mother of five in a blended family — the household went from three people to seven — Putnam said she kept running into the same problem: no product on the market let people of wildly different ages and abilities play together. “How can we use tech to create a shared experience?” is the question she said drove the pivot. It wasn’t a “movement from digital to analog,” as she put it, “so much as how can we use tech to bring people together rather than take them apart.”

It’s why Board’s touchscreen recognizes the physical objects placed on it — a spaceship triggers an action, a knife performs a cut — instead of relying on the buttons and joysticks of a traditional controller; this way, a child and a grandparent can play the same game without a shared learning curve.

Walker had the same instinct, but his came from anxiety about what AI is doing to work and to community. He started Heirloom, he said, because he was worried about AI “stealing knowledge work” and pulling people away from each other. If he was going to build something after Walker & Company, he wanted it to bring people back together.

It’s an interesting bet. Speaking at the same StrictlyVC event, Walker said he believes the U.S. has forgotten how to transmit mastery, including leatherworking, watchmaking, and fragrance design. For 50 years, he argued, America has broken the chain from master to apprentice, offshoring production and stripping the prestige from manual skill to the point that apprenticeships became something people did when they couldn’t get into a four-year college.

Heirloom is a wager that that’s now reversing, and Walker had a number to back it up, telling a room full of founders and investors that roughly half of Gen Z and Gen Alpha say they don’t want a four-year degree at all. In fact, more than half of the capacity at Heirloom’s first location in San Francisco is currently filled not by career-changers or retirees but by young tech workers looking for what he calls a “phones-down creative outlet.”

So far, the dollars involved are relatively small for these venture-backed startups. Putnam has raised [$35 million](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/02/board-the-new-game-startup-from-mirror-founder-brynn-putnam-raises-20m-has-already-sold-thousands/) from VCs for three-year-old Board. Pie has raised $24 million. Six Bells has raised roughly $3.8 million. Heirloom, founded 11 months ago, hasn’t disclosed its funding.

One possible exception is WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann, whose new residential real estate venture Flow — marketed around the same premise of solving loneliness through physical space — has raised more than [$450 million](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/24/report-adam-neumanns-flow-raises-100m-more-than-doubles-valuation-to-2-5b/), largely from Andreessen Horowitz, dwarfing everyone else in this story combined.

Indeed, right now it’s unclear whether “togetherness” becomes its own sizable investment category. Getting strangers to show up for each other — as good as that may be for society — isn’t nearly as scalable as shipping software.

What’s notable is who’s building these companies: Putnam, Walker, Dunn, Gelman, and Neumann have all built a real brand once before. That makes it easier to raise capital and gives investors some confidence these are founders who know how to build something people actually buy. They’ve each guessed right about where the puck is headed once before. We’ll know more in another year or two whether enough customers follow along again this time.

Artificial intelligence has cemented its place in the consumer shopping journey, with 80% of consumers reporting that they are somewhat or very comfortable relying on the technology to recommend products or services, per data from the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Shoppers have shown they have a preference for what sources AI cites, with 56% saying they favor recommendations that pull from creator or influencer reviews.

“Consumers are, more than ever, using AI for shopping and shopping recommendations. And what we found in this report is that consumers are looking for authenticity and trust and that is coming from creators,” said Jack Koch, senior vice president, research and insights at IAB.

IAB’s “The Creator Signal: How AI Systems Interpret Influence in Commerce” includes 2,200 survey respondents ages 16 and older who have used AI tools for shopping-related purposes in the last three months. It was conducted via the IAB Insights Engine, a research platform by Attest, in May 2026. Markets surveyed include the U.S., U.K., Australia , Mexico and India.

### **The creator divide**

Though the preference for creator content is evident, the sentiment is not shared equally across generations. For example, 65% of Gen Z and millennial respondents said they prefer when AI recommendations include creator and influencer sources, while 66% of boomers feel the opposite. Gen Xers are split, with 53% in favor of creator citations.

While consumers prefer chatbots to cite creators and influencers within its results, it is not the only source they believe the technology should rely on. Across generations, at least half of those surveyed believe chatbots should pull from consumer ratings and reviews. Consumer ratings and reviews are the most preferred source across generations for AI to leverage when it comes to what would increase their likelihood to purchase.

While younger consumers prefer when AI cites creator content, it doesn’t necessarily drive purchase. Just 29% of the Gen Zers and millennials surveyed said creators or influencer sources increased their likelihood of buying the product. That number fell to 12% when looking at boomers.

“I think the real story is, from a generational standpoint, once you get past subject matter experts, retailer or marketplace information, brand advertiser information, especially for younger generations, is really at the same place as creator influencer reviews,” said Koch.

Subject-matter experts, retail or marketplace information and brand or advertiser content consistently rank above creator or influencer reviews for AI source preference across generations. When looking at the sources preferred across all generations to increase consumers’ likelihood to purchase, subject-matter experts, retail or marketplace information and brand or advertiser content largely ranks above creator influencer reviews across all generations as well, however, for Gen Z respondents, creator or influencer reviews beat out retail or marketplace information by a single point.

### **The creator voice**

While consumers may find other sources more important during their AI shopping journey, it doesn’t mean brands should ignore creators completely. Consumers still find them valuable, with just 11% of respondents overall saying they do not find creator or influencer content helpful when included in AI recommendations, per the report. Additionally, 65% of respondents said credible creator reviews increase their confidence in AI recommendations.

Finding the best price or value was seen as the top area where respondents found influencers helpful, at a rate of 38%. Discovering new brands (32%), comparing products (31%) and summarizing product information (31%) were all identified as top areas where creator input was found to be helpful.

Respondents tend to favor influencer input in the early stages of the shopping journey, specifically around product discovery or initial research. Respondents didn’t find influencer input at the end stages of the purchasing journey to be as helpful, with 15% saying they found creators helpful when it came to completing or assisting with purchases and 21% with final purchase decisions.

Additionally, not all types of influencers are seen as equally valuable. Over half of respondents said AI should prioritize everyday consumers sharing real experiences and 43% said it should focus on professional product reviewers. Lifestyle creators (22%), journalists (17%) and celebrities or public figures (13%) ranked at the bottom.

Nearly half of respondents said a proven track record of credibility made an influencer or creator trustworthy enough for AI to rely on their content and 40% cited consistency over time. kept.heading: 5 LEVERS DRIVE CAC, SAYS AD PRO (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Lowering CAC on Meta and Google starts with giving platforms the right signals and creative. Ads should lead with novel hooks tied to customer pain points and use language that reflects the target audience. Brands should optimize for new-customer purchases rather than total purchases. Then, test creative across personas, angles, and formats. 5 levers ultimately drive CAC: the offer, creative, account structure, landing page, and optimization signals.
kept.article_text:
Title: 5 Levers Drive CAC, Says Ad Pro

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/5-levers-drive-cac-says-ad-pro

Published Time: 2026-09-18T14:00:58+00:00

Markdown Content:
Hal Smith says lowering clients’ customer acquisition cost on Meta and Google is a focus of his agency, H Street Digital. He cites 5 performance levers, starting with the offer.

Hal founded the D2C-centered agency in 2020 after stints managing political fundraising campaigns. “I learned the importance of the right message,” he told me.

In our recent conversation, Hal shared his approaches to ad messaging, testing, targeting, and, yes, reducing CAC. Our entire audio is embedded below. The transcript is edited for length and clarity.

**Eric Bandholz:** Who the heck are you?

**Hal Smith:** I’m the founder of H Street Digital in Austin, Texas. We manage performance marketing for direct-to-consumer brands, mostly in the outdoor space.

I started in political advertising, such as small-dollar grassroots fundraising. I learned the importance of the right message to get folks to donate to a candidate, a cause, or a committee.

I now focus on scaling D2C outdoor brands through advertising.

**Bandholz:** How much of ad performance is the marketing hook versus telling a brand’s story?

**Smith:** I have a couple of thoughts.

First, the top goal of advertising is to get someone to stop scrolling and click. And the best driver of that behavior is curiosity. Novelty creates a scroll stop because it’s something they haven’t seen. Some clients want very polished, professional-looking ads. The problem is that it’s not novel and is easy to overlook.

So it’s important to be intentional about how novel your creative concepts are versus brand constraints.

The second thing is hooks — the first three seconds of a video ad or the headline on a static ad. How do the hooks drive curiosity? We often lead with a question that’s specific to viewers or readers. It speaks to a pain point they might have. They get curious and want to know the answer.

There are a lot of tactics for that kind of storyboarding or scriptwriting. Figure out which part of a video or static ad drives the most interest. That becomes your hook.

**Bandholz:** How do you help brands understand that? A $5,000 photo shoot may not stand out.

**Smith:** We often see those glossy ads, especially on Meta, that don’t target the right customer. So our first step is to figure out the pain points merchants are trying to solve or the aspirations they’re trying to hit. Then we hone in on the language that those target prospects use to describe the pain point or need.

The final piece is ensuring the people in the ads actually reflect the target audience.

**Bandholz:** When do ads peter out and require new content?

**Smith:** I think about this question every day.

With creative, the biggest ad mistake that brands make is not optimizing for the right purchase event. In Meta and Google, brands typically go for the highest volume at the lowest price point. But that approach trains the platform to go after [any purchase](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/ditch-the-discount-says-brand-marketer).

What you want from the platforms is to get new customers. So the challenge is training the algorithms.

A better approach is to set up a custom purchase event for new customers and use it as your main optimization goal in Meta and Google. That creates a framework where the platforms have to work to reach new customers.

It also drives a creative testing strategy we call a matrix approach. Assemble all target customer personas, the main angles to reach them, and the formats. These could be static image ads, GIFs, user-generated videos, whitelisted or partnership ads, et cetera. But you need a large variety to cover enough of your target customers and know how to convert them.

Then you create that content.

If you test only the right purchase event, Meta and Google will tell you what creative is doing well.

**Bandholz:** A large variety. How many ads are we talking?

**Smith:** Aim for enough conversion actions in a given period, such as a week, to know confidently what’s working and what’s not.

You’re not learning anything with, say, a $500 daily budget and a $500 target acquisition cost. But if your target CAC is $20 and you’re spending $10,000 per day, you’re learning fast and can create much better variety.

So the ad volume depends on your budget and your target CAC.

**Bandholz:** How do brands lower CAC?

**Smith:** It’s a focus of our agency. In our experience, five performance levers impact CAC. Number one is the offer. A strong offer does a lot of the work to reduce cost.

The second is the creative. Compelling creative lowers CAC.

Next is the account structure. When auditing accounts, we often find brands have placed platform restrictions that limit learning.

The fourth is the [landing page](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/optimized-landing-pages-reduce-ad-costs). A high-converting landing page lowers CAC.

The fifth is signal engineering — setting the right targets for [Meta](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/cfo-brands-rarely-max-out-meta-ads) and Google to optimize for.

**Bandholz:** Cool. Where can people follow you, reach out, hire you?

**Smith:** Our site is [HStreetDigital.co](https://hstreetdigital.co/). Or message me on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hal-smith-hstreet/).

kept.heading: WHY BUILDING A FREE AUDIENCE IS KEEPING YOU BROKE (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Free audiences are much harder to monetize than paying customers. A campaign generated 3 paid subscribers from 7,500+ free readers versus 34 from roughly 350 existing customers. Instead of building an audience or product in isolation, build a small product, share the process publicly, and build relationships with potential customers. This creates distribution and trust while validating demand before scaling.
kept.article_text:
Title: Why "Build an Audience First" Fails (Do This Instead)

URL Source: https://theindiepreneur.substack.com/p/why-building-a-free-audience-is-keeping

Published Time: 2026-09-19T15:19:19+00:00

Markdown Content:
Let me tell you something, right off the bat:

I ran the same offer to two lists.

From 7,500+ free newsletter subscribers, I got 3 paid subscribers. 3.

From ~350 WriteStack customers (people who already pay me) I got 34 in 48 hours.

One converted 10% of the list. The other 0.042%.

MOST people get distribution completely wrong. And it makes sense, because everyone is pumping out the same thing: build an audience first. Then figure out what to sell them.

Or, better yet (not): build the product and if it’s good enough, people will come.

Both sound good. Both will lead you nowhere.

Distribution is the hardest part. If you already have people who listen and trust you, launching anything gets easier.

I tried both. Here’s what actually happened.

Back when I left my job as a software developer, I had no social platform that I was active on. So no followers anywhere. No audience at all.

As an employee in a tech company, I naturally gravitated towards LinkedIn. I remember being SO jealous of people who have 1,000+ followers. I felt like I'd missed the train and it would be impossible to catch up.

Nonetheless, that’s what I did for the next year or so. I built my LinkedIn audience. Got to 2,400.

But I still made $0, while people with fewer followers were making thousands a month.

Back then I didn’t know what I know now: I had 2,400 people watching and I never once asked any of them to buy anything. To be fair, I didn’t have anything to sell. I was building products the whole time, twelve of them, and every single one in stealth. My audience never heard about a single one more than once in a LinkedIn post.

An audience you never sell to is worth exactly as much as no audience. You get the likes. You get the nice comments. Nobody pays you.

The thing is, I was following the other advice at the same time. Build it and they will come. Just as badly

For 18 months I built over 12 products (before AI). I believed that if the idea was strong enough, people would just WANT to pay for it.

I mean, the logic makes sense. If you build a solution to people’s problems, they will inevitably want to pay for it to solve their issue. Or, as the _professionals_ say, scratch their itch.

So I followed this mantra, build it and they will come, for a year and a half. It got me from $0/month to: $0/month + epic frustration.

—

What you and Orel of 2 years ago need to understand is that people are complicated creatures. They first need to know you. Then they need to TRUST you. Then, and only then, they’ll bet on you and pay you for your product.

Especially when you don’t have a big brand or you don’t have the credentials.

As both methods failed, I had to try something different. And it started like every time. I built my idea.

But then I decided I was not going to give up if after 2 weeks nobody comes. I’m going to push it to 6 months. 6 months, 1 product.

So I started building relationships with people through DMs. Those relationships turned into TRUSTING relationships. And those TRUSTING relationships turned into paying users.

For the first time, after 18 months, I got paid for my products. It finally felt like I was doing something right.

But I still wasn’t 100% sure that it would work if I did it the second time, as I thought my audience was only there for WriteStack or free stuff.

I run two newsletters:

1.   TheIndiepreneur (7,000 subscribers)

2.   The Substack Data Analysis (800 subscribers)

Three months ago I turned on paid for the Data Report and sent the same short 3-email campaign to both free readers and WriteStack customers.

You already saw the scoreboard at the top. What matters is _why_ it split like that.

A free audience is a list of people who like free stuff. A paying audience is a list of people who trust you with their money. Trust with money compounds. Trust with attention is much harder to convert.

There are two exceptions. One of them probably isn’t you.

I want to be fair here, because it obviously works for some people. Sahil Bloom and Justin Welsh built huge free audiences and then sold to them.

Tom Orbach, the marketing genius who runs the popular MarketingIdeas newsletter, gave away so much free value that when he turned paid on, he became a bestseller almost overnight. Thousands of paid subscribers in a few months.

But look at what they had. Rare knowledge that was already valuable before they wrote a word.

Justin Welsh spent years as a sales executive, scaling a startup past $50M in revenue before he wrote his first LinkedIn post.

Sahil Bloom was a private equity investor who could explain finance to normal people, and that was the whole pitch.

Tom Orbach ran growth for one of the fastest-growing startups in the world before MarketingIdeas existed.

This insider experience most people can’t get anywhere else. Giving that away for free is a strategy because the free stuff is genuinely worth paying for.

If that’s you, go. Build the audience, be generous, sell later.

Most people starting out don’t have that. I didn’t. What I had was a journey I was going through. Nothing anyone would pay for yet. Which is why the second exception matters more.

Product number 13 was WriteStack. It’s the first one I built out loud.

At the start I had nothing to leverage. My Substack audience was solopreneurs, not the Substack writers WriteStack is for. So I brute-forced it through DMs and building relationships.

Once this distribution channel exhausted itself because more people came from word-of-mouth, I started working on bigger relationships.

I started sharing the building. Videos, the features I was adding, my face on camera explaining why.

I called it ‘Scaling WriteStack to 100k/year’.

First, credibility. Anyone who found WriteStack and then found me talking about it could see there was a real person building something that I care about (trust without contact).

Second, reach. When you share a feature, the people who want that feature notice. The bigger the audience got, the more chances I had to hit the people I was looking for.

This is what it took to build a product that makes $100K/year.

It’s not product first, then audience. It’s not audience first, then product. It’s the same activity. Building the thing gives you something to talk about. Talking about it brings the people. And by the time you ask them to pay, they already know what they’re paying for.

If you want an order, here it is:

1.   Build the thing. Small, ugly, doesn’t matter.

2.   Talk about building it.

3.   DM the people who react (and others)

4.   Get paid.

Now you have a list worth having. Repeat.

P.S.

I’m testing a small **90-day Substack accelerator** with a few writers who already publish and want to get to **1,000 subscribers** for real.

You’ll get a 90-day growth plan, direct feedback on your Notes and articles, and a WriteStack subscription while we work to put everything to use.

**3 spots.** Reply **accelerator** and I’ll send the details.

**Can't attend? Sign up anyway to be sent the recording.**

Rachel Duffy has watched Reddit go from "the platform you were scared to admit you used" to the industry's biggest opportunity.

Most publishers and brands still treat Reddit as a broadcast channel or, worse, a risk to be managed from a distance. Rachel has done the opposite: building real moderator relationships, understanding subreddit culture, and using the platform to drive genuine brand visibility and reader trust.

Join Rachel Duffy, Head of Community at The Times and Sunday Times, and founder of the Young Journalists Network, in this conversation with Rob Fawkes from Standing on Giants on what winning on Reddit actually looks like for a major media brand, and what any company can take from it.

**Rachel Duffy** is Head of Community at The Times and Sunday Times, having previously helped build the Telegraph's Reddit presence during their US election push. She's the founder of the Young Journalists Network, a community supporting early-career journalists, and has become one of the most recognised voices on Reddit strategy in UK media.
